1.summary: Yahweh calls the young Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, to be a prophet to the nations, touches his mouth, and shows him two visions, an almond branch and a boiling pot tipping from the north.
1.lookfor: Watch the pairs of verbs that describe Jeremiah's task, Jeremiah's objection and God's reply, and the two visions and the wordplay hidden in the first one.

names.name: Hilkiah
names.gloss: Jeremiah's father, a priest; probably not the high priest of the same name who found the law book in Josiah's temple.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: A village of priests about three miles north-east of Jerusalem, in Benjamin's territory.

names.name: Josiah
names.gloss: King of Judah (640–609 BC), remembered for his religious reform.

names.name: Jehoiakim
names.gloss: Josiah's son, king 609–598 BC, a bitter opponent of Jeremiah.

names.name: Zedekiah
names.gloss: Josiah's son and Judah's last king, whose reign ended with Jerusalem's fall.

insights.title: Forty years, three kings
insights.body: The heading dates Jeremiah's call to Josiah's thirteenth year, about 627 BC, and runs to the exile of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC (1:2-3). Those decades saw Assyria collapse, Josiah's reform rise and fail with his death, and Babylon take Judah. Jeremiah spoke through the whole slide, and the book follows him even beyond it, into Egypt.

insights.title: A priest's son from Anathoth
insights.body: Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his estate at Anathoth, ending that priestly line's role in Jerusalem. Many scholars think Jeremiah's family belonged to it, which would make him an outsider to the temple establishment he would later confront. The connection is likely but not certain.

insights.title: Known before birth
insights.body: God says he knew and set Jeremiah apart before he was formed in the womb (1:5). The servant in Isaiah 49 speaks the same way, and Paul echoes both when he describes God setting him apart from his mother's womb. The point in context is vocation: Jeremiah's calling is not his own idea.

insights.title: A prophet like Moses
insights.body: Jeremiah protests that he cannot speak and is only a youth (1:6), as Moses protested that he was slow of speech. God's answer, "I have put my words in your mouth" (1:9), echoes the promise of a prophet like Moses into whose mouth God would put his words. The book often presents Jeremiah as that kind of covenant spokesman.

insights.title: Almond and watching
insights.body: The almond is shaqed in Hebrew, and God says he is shoqed, watching, over his word to perform it (1:11-12). The almond blossoms first in the Israelite year, late in winter, as if keeping watch for spring. The vision is a pun, which the English cannot show.

insights.title: Six verbs for a career
insights.body: Jeremiah is set over nations to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant (1:10). Four verbs are for judgment and two for hope, and that balance matches the book. The same verbs return at turning points throughout it.

insights.title: The boiling pot from the north
insights.body: Armies from Mesopotamia reached Judah by following the Fertile Crescent and coming down from the north, because the desert blocked the direct route. The foe from the north (1:13-15) is left unnamed for many chapters; it is first identified as Babylon in 20:4.

insights.title: A fortified city of one man
insights.body: God promises to make Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls against kings, priests and people (1:18), yet the book will show him beaten, imprisoned and in despair. What does it mean that they will not prevail (1:19) when they so often seem to?

2.summary: Yahweh recalls Israel's early devotion and brings a legal case against the people for exchanging him, the spring of living water, for gods that cannot help.
2.lookfor: Watch the lawsuit language, the rapid string of images (bride, vine, cistern, camel, wild donkey), and the questions God puts to the people.

names.name: Kittim
names.gloss: Cyprus and the western coastlands, standing here for the far west.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: An Arabian desert tribe, standing for the far east.

names.name: Memphis
names.gloss: An ancient royal city of Egypt, near modern Cairo.

names.name: Tahpanhes
names.gloss: An Egyptian frontier fortress in the eastern Nile Delta.

names.name: Shihor
names.gloss: A branch of the Nile, or a stream on Egypt's border, standing for Egypt.

insights.title: A covenant lawsuit
insights.body: I will yet contend with you (2:9) translates riv, a word for a lawsuit or legal dispute. Prophets often framed God's complaint as a court case in which he lays out what he did and what the people did in return. Heaven itself is called as a witness (2:12).

insights.title: The wilderness honeymoon
insights.body: God remembers the love of Israel's youth, when the people followed him in the wilderness (2:2). Hosea, a century earlier, had used the same picture of the wilderness as a time of first love. Jeremiah draws heavily on Hosea's marriage imagery throughout chapters 2–3.

insights.title: Broken cisterns
insights.body: In the dry hills of Judah people cut cisterns into rock and lined them with plaster to store winter rain. A cracked cistern lost its water and left stagnant dregs. Israel has turned from a living spring to cisterns of its own making that cannot even hold water (2:13).

insights.title: Living water
insights.body: Living water in Hebrew means fresh, flowing water from a spring. Jeremiah calls Yahweh the spring of living waters again in 17:13. Jesus' offer of living water to the Samaritan woman and at the festival draws on this picture.

insights.title: Even the pagans keep their gods
insights.body: God tells the people to look west to Kittim and east to Kedar to find any nation that has changed its gods (2:10-11). Pagans stay loyal to gods that do not exist, yet Israel has exchanged its glory for what does not profit. Paul's phrase about people exchanging the glory of God may echo this verse.

insights.title: Egypt and Assyria
insights.body: Judah swung between Egypt and Assyria for protection (2:18, 2:36). Egypt's Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC and then made Judah a vassal, which may be the broken crown of 2:16. Leaning on great powers is treated as the political side of idolatry.

insights.title: Wood as father, stone as mother
insights.body: The people say to wood, You are my father, and to a stone, You gave birth to me (2:27). The wood is probably a sacred pole of Asherah and the stone a standing pillar, which were common at Canaanite shrines. Jeremiah's sarcasm reverses what one might expect, since Asherah was a goddess.

3.summary: Using the law of divorce, Yahweh pleads with unfaithful Israel and Judah to return, promising faithful shepherds and a future in which the ark is no longer needed.
3.lookfor: Watch the word return and its relatives, the contrast between the two sisters Israel and Judah, and the surprising picture of the future in 3:14-18.

insights.title: Can she go back?
insights.body: The chapter opens with the law that a divorced wife who marries another may not return to her first husband (3:1). By that rule Israel's case is closed. Yet God still says return to me, going beyond his own law in mercy.

insights.title: Two sisters
insights.body: The northern kingdom, Israel, fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Judah watched and did not learn (3:6-8). Dated to Josiah's day, this oracle says Judah's return under his reform was only in pretense (3:10), and so the fallen north looks more righteous than Judah (3:11).

insights.title: Turning and returning
insights.body: The Hebrew root shuv, to turn or return, runs through the chapter. Backsliding is meshuvah, a turning away; God calls shuvu, return; and promises to heal their turnings (3:22). Jeremiah uses this root more than any other book.

insights.title: No more ark
insights.body: God says the ark of the covenant will not be remembered or missed, nor will another be made (3:16), and all Jerusalem will be called Yahweh's Throne (3:17). The ark vanishes from the biblical record with the Babylonian conquest. Here its loss is pictured not as disaster but as something outgrown.

insights.title: Legends of the hidden ark
insights.body: Later Jewish tradition told how Jeremiah hid the ark before the city fell, a story found in 2 Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox churches count as Scripture. Other rabbinic traditions say Josiah hid it beneath the temple. Jeremiah 52 lists the temple treasures taken to Babylon but does not mention the ark.

insights.title: Shepherds after God's heart
insights.body: God promises shepherds according to my heart (3:15), language once used of David. In Jeremiah shepherds usually means kings and leaders, and the book returns to failed and faithful shepherds in chapter 23. The nations too will gather to Jerusalem (3:17).

insights.title: A confession prepared in advance
insights.body: The chapter ends with the words of repentance the people should say (3:22-25), as Hosea also supplied words for return. Is God writing their confession for them because they will not find it themselves, or showing how close return lies?

4.summary: Yahweh calls Judah to true repentance, then sounds the alarm as an invader comes from the north, and Jeremiah cries out in anguish at a vision of the land returned to chaos.
4.lookfor: Watch the switching voices (God, the prophet, the people), the trumpet and battle sounds, and the four I saw lines in 4:23-26.

names.name: Dan
names.gloss: Israel's northernmost town, the first place an invader from the north would reach.

insights.title: Circumcise your hearts
insights.body: Jeremiah calls the people to take away the foreskins of your heart (4:4), echoing Deuteronomy. The outward sign of the covenant needed an inward reality. Paul picks up the same idea when he says true circumcision is of the heart.

insights.title: Lion from the thicket
insights.body: The destroyer of nations is pictured as a lion leaving its lair (4:7). Lions still lived in the Jordan thickets. The lion was also a favorite royal symbol in Mesopotamia, and Babylon's processional way was lined with glazed lions.

insights.title: News coming south
insights.body: A voice declares from Dan, and then from the hills of Ephraim (4:15), only a short distance north of Jerusalem. The reports draw closer, as messengers bring word of an army marching south. The poetry lets the reader feel the enemy's approach.

insights.title: Has God deceived?
insights.body: Jeremiah protests that God has greatly deceived the people by letting them hear peace (4:10). Some read this as Jeremiah blaming the false prophets' message on God, who allowed it; others see real anguish that God's people were left unready. How far may a prophet argue with God?

insights.title: Without form and void
insights.body: Jeremiah sees the earth waste and void, tohu wavohu (4:23), the phrase used only here and in Genesis 1:2 for the world before creation. Light, mountains, people and birds are undone in reverse order. Judgment is pictured as creation running backward.

insights.title: The prophet's own heart
insights.body: My anguish, my anguish (4:19) translates a Hebrew cry about the bowels, the inner organs felt as the seat of emotion. Jeremiah feels the coming war physically. The book often blurs the line between his grief and God's.

insights.title: Yet not a full end
insights.body: Even in this vision of total ruin God adds, yet will I not make a full end (4:27). The phrase recurs in the next chapter and again in the promises of chapter 30. It is a small hinge on which the book's hope will turn.

5.summary: God sends Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for one honest person and finds none among rich or poor, so a far-off nation will come, though not to make a full end.
5.lookfor: Watch the search through the streets, the lists of what the invader will eat, and the contrast between the obedient sea and the rebellious people.

insights.title: Looking for one righteous person
insights.body: God offers to pardon Jerusalem if one person who acts justly can be found (5:1). Abraham bargained God down to ten righteous people for Sodom; here the price is one. The search fails among the poor and then among the great (5:4-5).

insights.title: The poor and the great
insights.body: Jeremiah first excuses the poor as ignorant and expects more of the leaders who know the law (5:4-5). But they too have broken the yoke. Later he praises Josiah for defending the poor and needy, which the leaders here neglect (5:28).

insights.title: A nation whose language you don't know
insights.body: The invader speaks a language Judah cannot understand (5:15), as the covenant curses in Deuteronomy warned. To ordinary Judeans the invaders' speech would sound like noise. The curse list of eaten crops and flocks also echoes Deuteronomy (5:17).

insights.title: The sea knows its limits
insights.body: God set the sand as a boundary for the sea (5:22). Even the roaring waves keep that line, while the people do not. The same picture of God setting limits for the sea appears in Job and the Psalms.

insights.title: Eyes that do not see
insights.body: The people are foolish, with eyes that don't see and ears that don't hear (5:21). Isaiah had spoken in the same way, and Jesus asks his disciples a similar question. The phrase describes refusal more than incapacity.

insights.title: Rain in its season
insights.body: Israel depended on the autumn and spring rains, which framed the growing season (5:24). Deuteronomy tied the rains to covenant faithfulness. Jeremiah says the people's sins have turned these gifts away (5:25).

insights.title: Fowlers and cages
insights.body: The wicked lie in wait like fowlers who set traps and fill cages with birds (5:26-27). Bird catching with nets and wicker cages was common. Here the trapped birds are people, and the houses are full of wealth gained by deceit.

insights.title: And my people love it
insights.body: The chapter ends not by blaming only the leaders: the prophets lie, the priests rule, and my people love to have it so (5:31). The book repeatedly makes false prophecy a two-way bargain between speakers and willing listeners.

6.summary: Jerusalem is besieged as an army arrives from the north, while its leaders cry peace where there is none, and Jeremiah is made an assayer of a people who prove to be dross.
6.lookfor: Watch the voices of the enemy soldiers planning their attack, the false word of peace, the call to the old paths, and the closing picture of refining silver.

names.name: Tekoa
names.gloss: A town in the hills about ten miles south of Jerusalem, home of the prophet Amos.

names.name: Beth Haccherem
names.gloss: A hilltop near Jerusalem, perhaps modern Ramat Rahel, used for signal fires.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A kingdom in south-west Arabia, famous for incense.

insights.title: Blow in Tekoa
insights.body: Blow the trumpet in Tekoa (6:1) is a pun in Hebrew: tiq'u, blow, sounds like Teqoa. Beth Haccherem means house of the vineyard. The people of Benjamin are told to flee south, away from the coming army.

insights.title: Siege mounds
insights.body: The enemy cuts trees and builds a mound against Jerusalem (6:6). Assyrian and Babylonian armies built earthen ramps to bring battering rams to the walls; the ramp at Lachish still survives. The soldiers' overheard voices plan to attack at noon and even at night (6:4-5).

insights.title: Peace, peace
insights.body: Prophets and priests treat the people's wound lightly, saying, "Peace, peace!" when there is no peace (6:14). The line is repeated in 8:11. The Hebrew shalom means wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of war.

insights.title: Rest for your souls
insights.body: God tells the people to ask for the old paths and walk in the good way to find rest for your souls (6:16). Jesus uses the same phrase when he invites the weary to take his yoke. The people reply simply, We will not walk in it.

insights.title: Incense from Sheba
insights.body: Frankincense from Sheba and fragrant cane from afar (6:20) were costly imports for worship. God rejects lavish offerings from people who reject his law (6:19). Earlier prophets had said the same, and Jeremiah's temple sermon in chapter 7 presses the point.

insights.title: Refining silver
insights.body: Silver was refined by melting ore with lead and blowing air across it, so that the lead carried away impurities. Jeremiah is a tester of metals (6:27), but the bellows blow and the lead is used up with no pure silver left (6:29). The people are rejected silver (6:30).

insights.title: Mourning as for an only son
insights.body: The daughter of my people must mourn as for an only son (6:26), the deepest grief in Israel. Amos and Zechariah use the same image. The book will later give the mourning its own voice in Lamentations, traditionally linked with Jeremiah.

7.summary: At the temple gate Jeremiah warns that the temple will not protect a people who break the commandments, and that God will do to it what he did to Shiloh.
7.lookfor: Watch the triple slogan the people repeat, the list of commandments being broken, the comparison with Shiloh, and the family worship of the queen of the sky.

names.name: Shiloh
names.gloss: The town north of Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood in the time of the judges and Samuel.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading tribe of the northern kingdom, standing for all of Israel's northern tribes, already exiled.

names.name: Topheth
names.gloss: A site in the valley of Hinnom where children were burned in sacrifice.

names.name: Hinnom
names.gloss: A valley just south and west of Jerusalem's walls.

insights.title: The temple sermon
insights.body: Chapter 26 tells the story of this same sermon, dated to the start of Jehoiakim's reign, around 609 BC, and records that it nearly cost Jeremiah his life. Josiah had just died in battle and his reform was unravelling. Jeremiah stands at the gate where worshippers pass (7:2).

insights.title: A slogan said three times
insights.body: The people repeat Yahweh's temple three times as a charm (7:4). A century earlier Jerusalem had been spared from Assyria in Hezekiah's day, and many concluded that God would never let his house fall. Jeremiah says the promise was never unconditional.

insights.title: Den of robbers
insights.body: The people break the commandments and then shelter in the temple, as robbers retreat to a den between raids (7:9-11). The list closely tracks the Ten Commandments, as Hosea's had done. Jesus quotes this verse when he drives the traders out of the temple, in a setting that also foretold its destruction.

insights.title: The ruin of Shiloh
insights.body: Shiloh had held the ark in Samuel's day (7:12). Scripture never narrates its fall directly, but Psalm 78 says God forsook it, and archaeologists have found evidence of destruction there in the 11th century BC, often linked with the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4. Jeremiah's hearers could still see its ruins.

insights.title: Cakes for the queen of the sky
insights.body: Whole families take part in making cakes for the queen of the sky (7:18). She was most likely a Mesopotamian or Canaanite goddess such as Ishtar or Astarte. In chapter 44 the women in Egypt insist that their troubles began when they stopped honoring her.

insights.title: Not sacrifices but obedience
insights.body: God says he did not command burnt offerings when Israel left Egypt, but obedience (7:22-23). Many readers take this as a Hebrew way of stating priority: not so much this as that. Others think it reflects the fact that the covenant at Sinai began with the commandments before the sacrificial laws.

insights.title: From Hinnom to Gehenna
insights.body: The valley of the son of Hinnom (7:31) was where children were burned at Topheth, and Josiah had defiled it to stop the practice. Its Hebrew name, ge hinnom, became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for the place of final judgment. Jeremiah renames it the valley of Slaughter (7:32).

insights.title: The voices fall silent
insights.body: God will silence the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (7:34), a picture of ordinary life ending. The line returns twice as a threat. In 33:11 it is reversed: the wedding songs will be heard again in the ruined city.

8.summary: Jeremiah grieves that Judah, unlike the migrating birds, does not know when to return, while its wise men and prophets offer false comfort; he asks if there is no balm in Gilead.
8.lookfor: Watch the questions in 8:4-5, the birds who keep their seasons, and the moment in 8:18-22 when it becomes hard to tell whether the prophet or God is grieving.

names.name: Dan
names.gloss: Israel's northern border town, where invaders were first heard.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hill country east of the Jordan, famous for its healing balm.

insights.title: Bones under the stars
insights.body: The bones of kings, priests and prophets will be spread before the sun, moon and stars they served (8:1-2). King Manasseh had built altars to the host of heaven in the temple courts, and Josiah tore them down. To be left unburied was the worst disgrace in the ancient world.

insights.title: The stork knows
insights.body: The stork, turtledove, swallow and crane observe their appointed time (8:7). The land of Israel lies on one of the world's great bird migration routes between Africa and Europe and western Asia, and huge flocks of storks pass through each spring and autumn. Birds return by instinct; Judah will not return at all.

insights.title: Return and turn away
insights.body: The questions in 8:4-5 play on the root shuv again: does one turn away and not return? Jerusalem has a perpetual backsliding, a turning that never turns back. Jeremiah's vocabulary of turning is one of his signatures.

insights.title: The scribes' false pen
insights.body: The wise say Yahweh's law is with us, but the false pen of the scribes has worked falsely (8:8). This is one of the earliest biblical references to a written law handled by scribes. Scholars debate whether Jeremiah means scribes distorting the law or people trusting a text while ignoring the word God now speaks.

insights.title: Repeated words of false peace
insights.body: Verses 8:10-12 repeat 6:12-15 almost exactly, including the cry of peace where there is no peace. Repetition is common in Jeremiah, perhaps because oracles were preached more than once and collected later. The repeated lines show how central false peace is to the book's charge.

insights.title: Balm in Gilead
insights.body: Gilead was known for a healing resin, which the Ishmaelite traders in Genesis carried to Egypt. The exact plant is uncertain. Jeremiah asks why, with balm and physicians near, his people are not healed (8:22); the answer lies in their refusal, not the lack of a cure.

insights.title: Whose grief is this?
insights.body: In 8:18-21 the speaker grieves for the daughter of my people, and in the middle God himself asks why they provoked him (8:19). The voices of prophet and God are woven together. Is Jeremiah's grief a window into God's own?

insights.title: The harvest is past
insights.body: The harvest is past, the summer has ended, and we are not saved (8:20) is a proverb-like lament. The grain harvest and then the summer fruit were the last chances for food before winter. The people waited for rescue through the season, and it did not come.

9.summary: Jeremiah longs to weep without end and to escape his deceitful people, God calls for mourning women to teach lament, and true boasting is found only in knowing Yahweh.
9.lookfor: Watch the language of the tongue and lies, the call for professional mourners, and the famous saying about boasting in 9:23-24.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Judah's neighbor and rival to the south-east, descended from Esau.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: A kingdom east of the Dead Sea.

insights.title: The weeping prophet
insights.body: Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a spring of tears (9:1). In the Hebrew Bible this verse is the last line of chapter 8, so it closes his lament there. Lines like it gave Jeremiah the title the weeping prophet.

insights.title: Every brother a Jacob
insights.body: Every brother will utterly supplant (9:4) is a pun in Hebrew: aqov ya'qov, every brother acts like Jacob. Esau had said Jacob supplanted him twice. The nation that carries Jacob's name has inherited his deceit.

insights.title: Professional mourners
insights.body: God tells the people to call the mourning women and the skilful women (9:17). In the ancient Near East, as still in some places, trained women led funeral laments with traditional chants. Here they are told to teach their daughters, because there will be many funerals (9:20).

insights.title: Death through the windows
insights.body: Death has come up into our windows (9:21). Some scholars hear an echo of a Canaanite myth in which Baal fears a window in his palace because Death might enter by it. Whether or not Jeremiah alludes to it, he pictures death as an intruder climbing into homes and taking children.

insights.title: Let him who boasts
insights.body: The wise, the mighty and the rich must not boast in themselves but in knowing Yahweh (9:23-24). Paul quotes the heart of this saying twice. In Jeremiah it is set amid judgment, as the one thing that will survive the loss of wisdom, power and wealth.

insights.title: Loving kindness
insights.body: God delights in loving kindness, justice and righteousness (9:24). Loving kindness translates hesed, covenant love that is loyal and generous. Knowing God means knowing what he is like and sharing his delight in these things.

insights.title: Uncircumcised in heart
insights.body: Judah is listed among nations like Egypt and Edom who practise circumcision but whose hearts are uncircumcised (9:25-26). The outward covenant sign does not set Judah apart if the inner life does not match. The corners of their hair cut off probably describes desert tribes with a distinctive haircut.

10.summary: Jeremiah mocks idols made of wood and metal that must be carried, praises Yahweh as the living God and maker of all, and laments as exile comes.
10.lookfor: Watch the contrast between the carved idols and the living God, the one verse in another language, and the shift to a lament at the end.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant port, probably in the far west of the Mediterranean, known for silver.

names.name: Uphaz
names.gloss: An unknown place named as a source of gold.

insights.title: Scarecrows in a cucumber field
insights.body: The idol is a tree cut down, decked with silver and gold and nailed so it won't fall over (10:3-5). Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115 make the same mockery. Jeremiah compares idols to a palm tree of turned work, which some translate as a scarecrow in a cucumber field.

insights.title: Signs of the sky
insights.body: The nations are dismayed at the signs of the sky (10:2). Babylon was the centre of ancient astrology, reading eclipses and the movements of planets as omens for kings. Israel is told that the heavens are God's work, not a source of fear.

insights.title: A verse in Aramaic
insights.body: Verse 10:11 is written in Aramaic, the international language of the age, not Hebrew. It is the only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah. It may be a ready-made sentence for exiles to say to their neighbours: the gods that did not make the heavens will perish.

insights.title: Silver from Tarshish
insights.body: Silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, clothed in blue and purple (10:9), describe the costliest materials. Blue and purple dyes came from murex shellfish and were extremely expensive. All this work is spent on something with no breath in it (10:14).

insights.title: The portion of Jacob
insights.body: The portion of Jacob is not like these (10:16). Portion, heleq, is the share of land each family received. Israel's share is God himself, and Israel is God's own inheritance.

insights.title: Two editions of the book
insights.body: The Greek Septuagint gives 10:1-16 in a shorter form and a different order, leaving out several verses of praise. Fragments of both forms of Jeremiah were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. This chapter is one of the clearest places to see that the book circulated in more than one edition.

insights.title: Correct me, but gently
insights.body: Jeremiah confesses that a person cannot direct his own steps and asks God to correct him with justice, not anger (10:23-24). He then asks God to pour out his wrath on the nations instead, words almost identical to Psalm 79. How do these two prayers sit side by side?

11.summary: Jeremiah proclaims the covenant's curses on a people who have broken it, is told not to pray for them, and discovers that the men of his own town are plotting to kill him.
11.lookfor: Watch the covenant language of 11:1-8, the command not to pray, and the first of Jeremiah's personal complaints to God from 11:18.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: Jeremiah's home village, where his own neighbors plot to kill him.

insights.title: The words of this covenant
insights.body: Jeremiah proclaims the words of this covenant (11:2) with language drawn from Deuteronomy. Many scholars link this to the law book found in the temple in 622 BC under Josiah. How far Jeremiah supported Josiah's reform is debated, but he plainly holds that a public renewal did not change hearts.

insights.title: Amen to the curses
insights.body: God says cursed is the man who does not hear the covenant, and Jeremiah answers Amen (11:3-5), as Israel did in the ceremony of curses at Mount Ebal. The iron furnace (11:4) for Egypt also comes from Deuteronomy. Jeremiah agrees with God's case even though it condemns his own people.

insights.title: As many gods as cities
insights.body: The charge that Judah has as many gods as cities repeats 2:28, and adds that Jerusalem has as many altars as streets (11:13). Excavations in Judah have found many small household figurines from this period, often thought to represent a goddess, which shows how common private worship was.

insights.title: The shameful thing
insights.body: Altars to the shameful thing (11:13) uses bosheth, shame, as a mocking substitute for the name Baal. Scribes did the same with names: Saul's son Eshbaal appears in Samuel as Ishbosheth. The writers refused to honor the god by name.

insights.title: Don't pray for this people
insights.body: For the second time God forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people (11:14). Prophets such as Moses and Samuel had interceded, and God had relented. What does it mean that a time can come when intercession is no longer heard?

insights.title: Like a gentle lamb
insights.body: Jeremiah says he was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter (11:19). The same picture appears in Isaiah's suffering servant, which the early church read of Jesus. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters have also seen Jeremiah as a model for the servant.

insights.title: The confessions begin
insights.body: In 11:18-12:6 Jeremiah begins a series of personal laments, often called his confessions, scattered through chapters 11–20. They are unique among the prophets for showing a prophet's inner struggle with his calling. They read much like the lament psalms.

insights.title: Your own village
insights.body: The men of Anathoth want Jeremiah silenced (11:21). A prophet condemning the nation brought shame and danger on his family and town, and he lived among priests who may have resented his attack on the temple. Jesus later said a prophet is not without honor except in his own country.

12.summary: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper, God answers that worse is to come, then laments forsaking his own house and promises a future even for Judah's hostile neighbors.
12.lookfor: Watch Jeremiah's question, God's unexpected reply about footmen and horses, and God's own voice of grief in 12:7-13.

insights.title: Why do the wicked prosper?
insights.body: Jeremiah grants that God is righteous and then asks why the treacherous thrive (12:1). Job, Psalm 73 and Habakkuk wrestle with the same question. Jeremiah's complaint is sharper because the wicked are those whom God himself planted (12:2).

insights.title: Footmen and horses
insights.body: God's answer is not an explanation but a harder question: if you are tired racing men on foot, how will you race horses? (12:5). The opposition of his village is only the start. Even his own family is against him (12:6).

insights.title: The pride of the Jordan
insights.body: The pride of the Jordan (12:5) means the dense thickets along the river, where lions and other animals lived. It was a dangerous place to travel. Jeremiah is told that a land of peace is easy compared with what lies ahead.

insights.title: God has forsaken his house
insights.body: God says, I have forsaken my house; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into her enemies' hands (12:7). The tone is grief, not cold anger. What does it say about God that he speaks of judging his people as losing what he loves most?

insights.title: A speckled bird
insights.body: Judah is like a speckled bird of prey attacked by other birds (12:9). Birds often mob one that looks different. The image may also suggest that Judah has become as predatory as the nations around it.

insights.title: Shepherds and the vineyard
insights.body: Many shepherds have trampled God's vineyard (12:10). Shepherds here are probably foreign rulers or Judah's own failed leaders. The vineyard echoes Isaiah's song of God's vineyard that bore wild grapes.

insights.title: Hope for the neighbors
insights.body: God will uproot Judah's hostile neighbors, but then have compassion and bring them back to their lands (12:14-15). If they learn to swear by Yahweh's name, they will be built up among his people (12:16). The promise anticipates the restoration oracles for Moab and Ammon later in the book.

13.summary: Jeremiah acts out God's message with a ruined linen belt, warns of a coming drunkenness of judgment, and tells the king and queen mother that their crowns have fallen.
13.lookfor: Watch the acted-out sign of the belt, the popular saying about wine jars turned against the hearers, and the question about the leopard's spots.

names.name: Euphrates
names.gloss: The great river of Mesopotamia, on the road to Babylon.

insights.title: Prophecy acted out
insights.body: The belt is the first of several sign-acts in Jeremiah, in which the prophet performs a message as well as speaking it. A linen belt worn close to the body pictures Israel clinging to God (13:11), and linen was also the material of priests' garments. Once hidden and left, it is ruined (13:7).

insights.title: Which Euphrates?
insights.body: The Hebrew name is Perath, normally the Euphrates (13:4), which was hundreds of miles away and a journey of months there and back. Some scholars suggest a spring at Parah, a few miles from Anathoth, chosen for its name; others take the journeys as visionary. Either way the river points to Babylon, where Judah's pride will rot.

insights.title: A saying everyone knows
insights.body: Every jar should be filled with wine (13:12) sounds like a tavern proverb, and the people answer that of course it should. God turns it into a threat: the people themselves are the jars, and he will fill them with a drunkenness that sends them crashing into each other (13:13-14).

insights.title: The queen mother
insights.body: In Judah the king's mother held an official title and real influence. The king and queen mother here are most likely Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, who were taken to Babylon together in 597 BC. Their crowns have come down (13:18).

insights.title: Leopard's spots
insights.body: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? (13:23). The point is not about skin color but about habit: Judah has practised evil so long that it can no more change than a person can change his skin. The image became proverbial in English.

insights.title: Weeping in secret
insights.body: If they will not listen, Jeremiah says, my soul will weep in secret for your pride (13:17). The prophet who announces judgment is the one who mourns it most. Is there any way to deliver hard words faithfully without that grief?

insights.title: Shame uncovered
insights.body: Jerusalem's skirts are lifted over her face (13:22, 13:26). The image draws on the public shaming of an unfaithful wife and on the stripping of captives. It is harsh language, used by several prophets, for the exposure of conquest.

14.summary: In a severe drought the people lament and appeal to God, but he tells Jeremiah not to pray for them and condemns the prophets who promise peace.
14.lookfor: Watch the vivid scenes of drought, the prayers of the people in 14:7-9 and 14:19-22, and God's replies to each.

insights.title: A land without rain
insights.body: The drought reaches everyone: nobles' servants find empty cisterns, farmers face cracked ground, the doe abandons her fawn and the wild donkeys pant on the heights (14:3-6). In a land with no major rivers, failed winter rains meant famine. Deuteronomy listed drought among the covenant curses.

insights.title: A lament liturgy
insights.body: The chapter is built like a public service: a description of disaster, a confession and plea from the people (14:7-9), God's answer, a second plea (14:19-22) and a final answer in the next chapter. The people say the right words, but God rejects them as empty (14:10).

insights.title: The hope of Israel
insights.body: The people call God the hope of Israel, its Savior in time of trouble (14:8). They ask why he acts like a traveler who stops for one night and moves on. Paul later said he was in chains for the hope of Israel.

insights.title: Not even prayer
insights.body: For the third time God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people's good (14:11), and he rejects their fasts and offerings (14:12). Jeremiah keeps praying anyway. What does it say about him, and about God, that he does not stop?

insights.title: Assured peace
insights.body: The prophets promise assured peace in this place (14:13). God says he never sent them; their visions come from their own hearts (14:14). The clash between Jeremiah and these prophets becomes open conflict in chapters 23 and 28.

insights.title: For your name's sake
insights.body: The people appeal to God's name and to the throne of your glory, meaning the temple (14:21). Appealing to God's reputation among the nations is common in laments. They end by confessing that no idol can send rain; only Yahweh can (14:22).

insights.title: Sword, famine and pestilence
insights.body: Sword, famine and pestilence (14:12) is a triad that appears over a dozen times in Jeremiah. It describes the stages of a siege: battle outside, hunger within, then disease. Drought is a foretaste of the siege to come.

15.summary: God refuses even the prayers of Moses and Samuel for Judah, and Jeremiah, cursed by everyone, complains bitterly; God calls him to return and renews his promise of protection.
15.lookfor: Watch the reasons God gives for judgment, the turn to Jeremiah's own lament in 15:10, and God's surprising call for the prophet himself to return.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: King of Judah (about 697–642 BC) whose long reign was remembered for idolatry and bloodshed.

names.name: Hezekiah
names.gloss: Manasseh's father, a faithful king of Judah.

insights.title: Moses and Samuel
insights.body: Moses and Samuel were Israel's great intercessors, whose prayers turned God's anger aside. Even they could not change the verdict now (15:1). Jeremiah is placed in their line, as a prophet who prays, but the moment for intercession has passed.

insights.title: Because of Manasseh
insights.body: God says the exile comes because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (15:4). The book of Kings also blames Manasseh, whose idolatry and shedding of innocent blood outweighed Josiah's reform. Jeremiah balances this elsewhere by insisting each generation added its own sins (16:12).

insights.title: Mother of seven
insights.body: She who has borne seven languishes (15:9). Seven sons were a picture of complete blessing, as in Hannah's song. Here the blessed mother loses them all, and her sun sets while it is still day.

insights.title: A man of strife
insights.body: Jeremiah wishes he had never been born, since he has become a man of contention to the whole land (15:10). He has not been a lender or a borrower, the two roles that usually caused quarrels. Everyone curses him simply for his message.

insights.title: Eating God's words
insights.body: Your words were found, and I ate them (15:16). Ezekiel and John are given scrolls to eat in visions. For Jeremiah the image describes taking God's word into himself, and it brought joy before it brought loneliness (15:17).

insights.title: A deceitful brook
insights.body: Jeremiah asks if God will be to him like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail (15:18). A wadi in Israel runs full after rain and then dries up in summer, disappointing travelers who counted on it. It is a startling thing to say to the one he earlier called the spring of living waters.

insights.title: Even the prophet must return
insights.body: God answers Jeremiah's complaint by calling him to return and to separate the precious from the worthless (15:19). Only then will he be God's mouth. The renewed promise of a bronze wall repeats his call in chapter 1. Why does God answer a hurting prophet with a call to repent?

insights.title: Return to you, not to them
insights.body: The root shuv appears four times in 15:19: if you return, I will restore you; they will return to you, but you will not return to them. Jeremiah must not turn toward the people's views to win them; they must turn toward God's word.

16.summary: God forbids Jeremiah to marry, to mourn or to feast, as signs of the coming disaster, yet promises a new exodus from the north and that the nations will come to him.
16.lookfor: Watch the three things Jeremiah must not do, the reasons God gives, and the sudden promise in 16:14-15 and 16:19-21.

insights.title: A prophet with no family
insights.body: Jeremiah is told not to marry or have children (16:2), which was highly unusual in Israel, where family was central to a man's life and name. His single life becomes a sign that children born in the land will die. Hosea's marriage and Ezekiel's widowhood were also signs.

insights.title: Funeral customs
insights.body: Mourners cut themselves or shaved their heads, broke bread for the grieving and offered a cup of consolation (16:6-7). The law forbade the cutting and shaving, but they were evidently still practised. Soon there will be too many dead for any of these rites.

insights.title: No house of feasting
insights.body: Jeremiah may not go to a funeral or a feast (16:5, 16:8). He stands apart from both grief and joy, as the voices of bridegroom and bride will soon be silenced (16:9). His absence from community life is itself a message.

insights.title: A new exodus
insights.body: People will no longer swear by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt but by the God who brought them back from the north (16:14-15). The return from exile will be so great that it eclipses the exodus. The promise is repeated in 23:7-8.

insights.title: Fishers and hunters
insights.body: God will send fishermen and hunters to search out his people from every hiding place (16:16). Here the image is of judgment, leaving nowhere to hide. Jesus' call to his disciples to be fishers of men turns a related image toward gathering people in.

insights.title: Double for their sin
insights.body: God will repay their sin double (16:18). The Hebrew may mean twice over or, as some scholars argue, the full equivalent. Isaiah 40 later announces that Jerusalem has received double for all her sins and that her term is over.

insights.title: The nations come
insights.body: Jeremiah's prayer imagines nations from the ends of the earth confessing that their fathers inherited only lies (16:19). Just when Judah is being exiled for idolatry, Gentiles are pictured abandoning theirs. How does the book hold judgment on Israel and hope for the nations together?

17.summary: Judah's sin is engraved on their hearts, the one who trusts God is like a well-watered tree, the heart is deceitful, Jeremiah prays for healing, and the Sabbath is set as a test.
17.lookfor: Watch the contrast of desert bush and riverside tree, the saying about the heart, Jeremiah's prayer in 17:14-18, and the conditions of the Sabbath sermon.

names.name: Asherah
names.gloss: Wooden poles or trees honoring the Canaanite goddess Asherah, set up at shrines.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: The tribal territory just north of Jerusalem, Jeremiah's home region.

insights.title: Written with an iron pen
insights.body: Judah's sin is written with an iron pen and a diamond point on their hearts and on the horns of their altars (17:1). Stone inscriptions were cut with metal or hard-stone tools. The horns, corner projections on altars, were where sacrificial blood was smeared for atonement, but here they hold a record of sin.

insights.title: The tree by the water
insights.body: The one who trusts in man is like a desert shrub, while the one who trusts in Yahweh is like a tree with roots by the stream (17:5-8). Psalm 1 uses the same picture for the one who delights in God's law. Jeremiah's tree keeps bearing fruit even in drought.

insights.title: The deceitful heart
insights.body: The heart is deceitful above all things (17:9). Deceitful translates aqov, from the same root as the name Jacob and the supplanting of 9:4. In Hebrew thought the heart is the centre of thought and will, not only feeling, and only God can search it (17:10).

insights.title: The partridge's eggs
insights.body: A man who gets rich unjustly is like a partridge sitting on eggs she did not lay (17:11). This probably reflects a popular belief about the bird, or the fact that brooded eggs are often lost. Either way, ill-gotten wealth will not stay.

insights.title: Written in the dust
insights.body: Those who turn away from God will be written in the earth (17:13), a record that soon disappears, unlike names written in a book. Some interpreters connect this with Jesus writing on the ground before the woman's accusers, though the Gospel does not say what he wrote.

insights.title: Where is the word?
insights.body: Jeremiah's opponents mock him: Where is Yahweh's word? Let it come now (17:15). His warnings had not yet come true, which made him look like a false prophet by the test of Deuteronomy 18. He insists he never wanted the day of disaster (17:16).

insights.title: The Sabbath at the gates
insights.body: Jeremiah is sent to the city gates to call for the Sabbath to be kept by not carrying loads through them (17:21-22). Keeping it will mean kings on David's throne and a lasting city; breaking it, fire in the gates (17:25-27). Nehemiah later shut the gates on the Sabbath and recalled that such sins brought the disaster.

18.summary: At the potter's house Jeremiah learns that God can reshape a nation as clay, depending on how it responds, but the people refuse and plot against Jeremiah, who prays bitterly against them.
18.lookfor: Watch what the potter does with the spoiled pot, the two conditional cases in 18:7-10, the people's reply, and Jeremiah's response to the plot.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel, snow-capped for much of the year.

insights.title: The potter's wheel
insights.body: The potter works on the wheels (18:3), literally the two stones. Ancient potters used a pair of stone discs on an axle, the lower one turned by the feet and the upper one shaping the clay. A marred pot could be squashed and reshaped while the clay was still soft.

insights.title: Prophecy with conditions
insights.body: If a nation threatened with judgment repents, God will relent; if a nation promised blessing turns to evil, he will reconsider the good (18:7-10). This is a key passage for how prophecy works: many warnings are invitations, not fixed forecasts. The book of Jonah shows the first case.

insights.title: The potter and the clay
insights.body: Paul uses the potter and the clay to speak of God's freedom. In Jeremiah the image stresses both God's power and his responsiveness: the clay's response matters to what the potter does. The people still answer, It is in vain (18:12).

insights.title: Snow that never fails
insights.body: Does the snow leave Lebanon's rocks, or the cold streams dry up? (18:14). Nature is reliable, but Judah is not. It has left the ancient paths for byways (18:15), echoing the old paths of 6:16.

insights.title: Hissing and head-shaking
insights.body: The land will become a perpetual hissing, and passers-by will shake their heads (18:16). Whistling and head-shaking were gestures of shock and scorn at a ruin. The same gestures were made at Jesus on the cross.

insights.title: Priest, wise man and prophet
insights.body: The plotters say that law from the priest, counsel from the wise and the word from the prophet will not fail (18:18). These were Judah's three recognized sources of guidance. They are confident they can do without Jeremiah.

insights.title: A prayer for vengeance
insights.body: Jeremiah asks God to give his enemies' children to famine and not to forgive their sins (18:21-23). He reminds God that he once prayed for these same people (18:20). Like the cursing psalms, it gives raw words to betrayal and hands vengeance to God. How should readers who also know Jesus' prayer for his killers read it?

19.summary: Jeremiah takes a clay jar to the valley of Hinnom, announces judgment for child sacrifice, and smashes the jar as a sign that Jerusalem will be broken beyond repair.
19.lookfor: Watch the difference between this fired jar and the soft clay of chapter 18, the setting at the Potsherd Gate, and where Jeremiah goes when he has finished.

names.name: Harsith
names.gloss: A Jerusalem gate, probably the Potsherd Gate where broken pottery was dumped, leading to the valley of Hinnom.

names.name: Topheth
names.gloss: The site in the valley of Hinnom where children were burned in sacrifice.

insights.title: Clay that can no longer change
insights.body: In chapter 18 soft clay could be reshaped. Here the jar is already fired, and once smashed it can't be made whole again (19:11). The two potter scenes side by side show the window for change closing.

insights.title: A gurgling jar
insights.body: The jar is a baqbuq, a narrow-necked flask whose name imitates the gurgle of liquid poured from it. God says he will make void the plans of Judah (19:7), baqqothi, a play on the jar's name. The broken flask pictures plans emptied out.

insights.title: Tingling ears
insights.body: Disaster that makes every hearer's ears tingle (19:3) was said of the fall of Eli's house at Shiloh and of the judgment announced for Manasseh's sins. The phrase links Jerusalem's fate to both.

insights.title: Child sacrifice
insights.body: Judah's kings had built high places to burn their sons as offerings (19:5). Ahaz and Manasseh are said to have done so, and Josiah defiled Topheth to stop it. The text insists three times that God never commanded or imagined such a thing.

insights.title: Siege hunger
insights.body: The warning that people will eat their own children in the siege (19:9) quotes the covenant curses of Deuteronomy. Ancient sieges could last many months, and records from several cultures describe such horrors. Lamentations later reports that it happened in Jerusalem.

insights.title: The potter's field
insights.body: Matthew credits Jeremiah when he describes Judas' silver buying the potter's field. Matthew's wording comes mostly from Zechariah, but the potter, the valley and a field of burial recall this chapter and Jeremiah's land purchase in chapter 32. Matthew seems to blend them under the name of the greater prophet.

insights.title: From the valley to the temple
insights.body: After the sign in the valley, Jeremiah repeats the message in the temple court (19:14-15). This public challenge to the temple leadership leads directly to his arrest in the next chapter.

20.summary: The temple officer Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks; Jeremiah renames him and then pours out to God the most anguished of his complaints, ending with a curse on the day he was born.
20.lookfor: Watch the new name Jeremiah gives Pashhur, the first naming of Babylon, and the swings between complaint, trust, praise and despair in 20:7-18.

names.name: Pashhur
names.gloss: A priest of the Immer family and chief officer of the temple.

names.name: Immer
names.gloss: Head of one of the priestly families.

names.name: Magormissabib
names.gloss: The name Jeremiah gives Pashhur, meaning terror on every side.

insights.title: The stocks
insights.body: Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks at the upper Benjamin gate of the temple (20:2). The Hebrew word suggests a device that held the body twisted or bent. Being displayed in a gate added public humiliation to pain.

insights.title: Terror on every side
insights.body: Jeremiah renames Pashhur Magormissabib, terror on every side (20:3). The phrase is one of his favorites, recurring in 6:25 and in oracles against Egypt and Kedar. His enemies even use it to mock him (20:10), and Psalm 31 uses it of an innocent sufferer.

insights.title: Babylon is named
insights.body: Here, for the first time in the book, the foe from the north is named: the king of Babylon (20:4). From this point Babylon dominates the book. The vague threat has become a specific empire.

insights.title: Persuaded, or seduced
insights.body: You have persuaded me, and I was persuaded (20:7) uses pathah, a verb that can mean to entice, deceive or even seduce, as in the law about a man who seduces a virgin. Translations range from persuaded to deceived. Jeremiah says God overpowered him into a calling that has made him a laughingstock.

insights.title: Fire in the bones
insights.body: If Jeremiah tries to stop speaking, God's word is like a burning fire shut up in my bones (20:9). He cannot hold it in. Amos and Paul describe the same compulsion to speak.

insights.title: Cursing the day of birth
insights.body: Jeremiah curses the day he was born and the man who brought the news (20:14-15), much as Job curses his birthday. He wishes his mother's womb had been his grave (20:17). The cities that God overthrew (20:16) are Sodom and Gomorrah.

insights.title: Praise, then curse
insights.body: The prayer moves from accusation to trust (20:11), to praise (20:13), and then straight to cursing his birth (20:14). Some scholars think the sections were placed together by editors; others see the honest swings of a real sufferer. What does it mean that Scripture leaves the despair as the last word here?

21.summary: During Babylon's siege King Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to seek a miracle, but Jeremiah answers that God himself is fighting against the city and that those who surrender will live.
21.lookfor: Watch what Zedekiah hopes for, how God's answer reverses the language of the exodus, and the choice set before the people in 21:8-9.

names.name: Zedekiah
names.gloss: Judah's last king, put on the throne by Babylon in 597 BC.

names.name: Pashhur
names.gloss: Pashhur son of Malchijah, a royal official, not the temple officer of chapter 20.

names.name: Zephaniah
names.gloss: A senior priest, son of Maaseiah, often sent between the king and Jeremiah.

names.name: Nebuchadnezzar
names.gloss: King of Babylon (605–562 BC), who took Jerusalem twice.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The ruling people of the Babylonian empire, originally from southern Mesopotamia.

insights.title: A jump in time
insights.body: The book now leaps about twenty years, to the siege that began in 588 BC under Zedekiah. Jeremiah's book is arranged by theme more than date. Chapters 21–23 gather oracles about Judah's kings and prophets.

insights.title: Hoping for a repeat
insights.body: Zedekiah hopes God will act according to all his wondrous works (21:2) and make Babylon withdraw. He likely had in mind Hezekiah's day, when Assyria's army withdrew from Jerusalem. Jeremiah's answer is that this time there will be no rescue.

insights.title: The exodus reversed
insights.body: God says he will fight against Judah with an outstretched hand and a strong arm (21:5). Deuteronomy describes the exodus with a strong hand and outstretched arm. The same power that once rescued Israel is now turned against it.

insights.title: The way of life and death
insights.body: God sets before the people the way of life and the way of death (21:8), echoing Moses' choice at the edge of the promised land. But here life means surrendering to the Chaldeans (21:9). To many it sounded like treason.

insights.title: Surrender as faithfulness
insights.body: Jeremiah urged people to desert to the enemy, and officials later demanded his death for weakening morale. He saw Babylon as God's instrument and resistance as resisting God. How do readers tell faithful realism from defeatism?

insights.title: Justice in the morning
insights.body: The house of David is told to execute justice in the morning (21:12). Kings and judges heard cases at the city gate early in the day, before the heat. Delaying justice let the powerful keep what they had taken.

insights.title: The rock of the plain
insights.body: God speaks against the inhabitant of the valley and the rock of the plain who say no one can come against them (21:13). Jerusalem sat on a rocky ridge surrounded by valleys and felt secure. The oracle mocks its confidence in its natural defences.

22.summary: Jeremiah warns the royal house to do justice, mourns King Shallum's exile, condemns Jehoiakim's luxury built with unpaid labor, and declares that no descendant of Coniah will rule on David's throne.
22.lookfor: Watch the three kings named in turn, the contrast between Jehoiakim and his father Josiah, and the image of the signet ring.

names.name: Shallum
names.gloss: Another name for Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, who reigned three months in 609 BC before Egypt deported him.

names.name: Jehoiakim
names.gloss: Josiah's son, king 609–598 BC.

names.name: Coniah
names.gloss: A short form of Jehoiachin, Jehoiakim's son, who reigned three months before Babylon deported him in 597 BC.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: The fertile highlands east of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Abarim
names.gloss: The mountain range east of the Dead Sea, including Mount Nebo.

insights.title: Weep for the one who goes
insights.body: Don't weep for the dead, but for him who goes away (22:10). The dead king is Josiah, killed at Megiddo in 609 BC; the one who goes is his son Shallum, also called Jehoahaz, whom Pharaoh Neco took to Egypt where he died (22:11-12).

insights.title: A palace built on unpaid labor
insights.body: Jehoiakim builds a spacious palace with large windows, cedar panelling and red paint, using neighbors' work without wages (22:13-14). He did so while paying heavy tribute to Egypt. Some archaeologists have linked a lavish palace found at Ramat Rahel, just south of Jerusalem, with Jehoiakim's reign, though this is debated.

insights.title: This is to know me
insights.body: God says of Josiah: he judged the cause of the poor and needy. Wasn't this to know me? (22:16). In Jeremiah knowing God is not only right belief but practising justice. Jehoiakim's eyes are only on gain (22:17).

insights.title: The burial of a donkey
insights.body: Jehoiakim will have the burial of a donkey, dragged out and thrown beyond the gates (22:19). The book of Kings says only that he slept with his fathers, which usually means a normal death. Scholars debate whether the prophecy was fulfilled literally, perhaps during the siege when his body could not be buried properly.

insights.title: The signet ring
insights.body: A signet ring was a king's seal and signature, worn close and guarded carefully. Even if Coniah were God's signet ring, God would pull it off (22:24). Haggai later reverses this when God calls Zerubbabel, Coniah's grandson, his signet ring.

insights.title: Write him childless
insights.body: Coniah is to be recorded as childless (22:30), yet Chronicles lists his sons. The verse explains that none of them will prosper on David's throne. Babylonian ration tablets from Nebuchadnezzar's palace list oil for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and his sons in exile. Matthew includes him in Jesus' genealogy, which Christian interpreters have discussed in light of this verse.

insights.title: O land, land, land
insights.body: The threefold cry, O earth, earth, earth (22:29), calls the whole land to witness. Triple repetition gives the strongest possible emphasis in Hebrew, as in Yahweh's temple three times in 7:4.

23.summary: God condemns Judah's shepherds and promises a righteous Branch from David, then speaks at length against prophets who speak their own dreams instead of his word.
23.lookfor: Watch the wordplay in the name of the coming king, the test of a true prophet in 23:18-22, and the images of straw, fire and hammer.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: The capital of the former northern kingdom of Israel.

names.name: Gomorrah
names.gloss: The city destroyed with Sodom in Genesis, a byword for wickedness.

insights.title: Shepherds and the flock
insights.body: Woe to the shepherds who scatter the sheep (23:1). God will gather the remnant himself and set up good shepherds (23:3-4). Ezekiel 34 develops the same picture at length, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd.

insights.title: The righteous Branch
insights.body: God will raise up for David a righteous Branch (23:5), tsemah, a sprout growing from a stump. The term became a title for the coming king in Zechariah. Jewish and Christian traditions alike have read it messianically, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus.

insights.title: A pun on Zedekiah
insights.body: The king will be called Yahweh our righteousness (23:6), Yahweh tsidqenu. Zedekiah's name, Tsidqiyahu, means Yahweh is my righteousness. The coming king will be what Zedekiah's name promised but his reign never delivered.

insights.title: Standing in the council
insights.body: A true prophet has stood in the council of Yahweh (23:18, 23:22). Israel pictured God surrounded by a heavenly court, and prophets as messengers who had overheard its decisions. The false prophets were never there.

insights.title: Peace to the stubborn
insights.body: The false prophets tell those who despise God, you will have peace (23:17). Their message comforts people in sin rather than calling them to turn (23:22). That is Jeremiah's main test: a true word turns people from evil.

insights.title: Fire and hammer
insights.body: What is the straw to the wheat? God's word is like fire, and like a hammer that breaks rock (23:28-29). Dreams are not condemned in themselves, but dreams passed off as God's word are chaff beside the real grain.

insights.title: The burden of Yahweh
insights.body: The Hebrew massa means both an oracle and a burden. When people ask for the massa of Yahweh, God answers that they are the burden, and he will cast them off (23:33). The WEB uses message, which hides the pun; the Greek translators read the line as you are the burden.

insights.title: A God near and far
insights.body: Am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off? (23:23). The false prophets assumed a God close and manageable. God insists he fills heaven and earth (23:24). Is it possible to stress God's nearness in a way that shrinks him?

24.summary: In a vision of two baskets of figs, God declares that the exiles taken to Babylon in 597 BC are the good figs he will bring back, while Zedekiah and those left in Jerusalem are the bad.
24.lookfor: Watch which group is called good and which bad, and how the promises to the good figs echo Jeremiah's call in chapter 1.

names.name: Jeconiah
names.gloss: Another form of Jehoiachin or Coniah, the king taken to Babylon in 597 BC.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The ruling people of Babylon.

insights.title: After the first deportation
insights.body: In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar took King Jeconiah, the officials and the skilled craftsmen and smiths to Babylon (24:1). Zedekiah was left to rule a reduced Judah. Removing craftsmen and smiths also removed the ability to make weapons.

insights.title: First-ripe figs
insights.body: The good figs are like those first ripe (24:2), the early figs of late spring that were a delicacy. Bad figs that cannot be eaten were simply rotten. The vision may have been prompted by baskets of first fruits brought to the temple.

insights.title: A shocking reversal
insights.body: Those left in Jerusalem assumed they were God's favored remnant and the exiles were cursed. Jeremiah says the opposite (24:5, 24:8). Ezekiel, among the exiles, reports the same argument.

insights.title: A heart to know me
insights.body: God will give the exiles a heart to know me, and they will be my people and I their God (24:7). This anticipates the new covenant of 31:31-34. Return to the land is joined to an inner change that God himself gives.

insights.title: Build and plant
insights.body: God will build and not pull down, plant and not uproot (24:6). The verbs of Jeremiah's call return, now applied to the exiles. The hopeful half of his commission begins to take shape among the people already in Babylon.

insights.title: What do you see?
insights.body: God asks, What do you see, Jeremiah? (24:3), as at the almond branch and boiling pot. Amos too saw a basket of summer fruit. The pattern of everyday object, question and divine explanation was a familiar way of receiving a vision.

insights.title: Not the end of the story
insights.body: The good figs are not good because they were better people but because God sets his eyes on them for good (24:6). The bad figs include those who will flee to Egypt (24:8). Does the vision describe God's choice, the people's response, or both?

25.summary: After twenty-three years of unheeded preaching, Jeremiah announces seventy years of Babylonian rule and is made to pass the cup of God's wrath to Judah and all the nations, ending with Babylon itself.
25.lookfor: Watch the date at the start, the title God gives Nebuchadnezzar, the length of the exile, and the long list of nations who must drink the cup.

names.name: Uz
names.gloss: A land east or south-east of Israel, Job's homeland, perhaps near Edom.

names.name: Ashkelon
names.gloss: A Philistine port on the Mediterranean coast.

names.name: Dedan
names.gloss: An oasis trading centre in north-west Arabia.

names.name: Tema
names.gloss: An oasis town in north-west Arabia.

names.name: Elam
names.gloss: A kingdom east of Babylon in what is now south-west Iran.

names.name: Medes
names.gloss: A people of north-western Iran who later helped topple Assyria and joined Persia.

names.name: Sheshach
names.gloss: A coded name for Babylon.

insights.title: The year of Carchemish
insights.body: The fourth year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar's first (25:1), is 605 BC. That year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish on the Euphrates and became king, making Babylon master of the region. Jeremiah looks back on twenty-three years of preaching since 627 BC (25:3).

insights.title: Nebuchadnezzar, my servant
insights.body: God calls the pagan king my servant (25:9), a title usually given to Moses, David and the prophets. It does not mean Nebuchadnezzar worshipped Yahweh, but that he was carrying out God's purpose. Isaiah calls Cyrus God's anointed in a similar way.

insights.title: Seventy years
insights.body: The nations will serve Babylon seventy years (25:11). Some count from 605 BC to Cyrus' decree in 538, others from the temple's destruction in 586 to its rebuilding in 516; many see it as a round number for a lifetime. Later writers in Chronicles, Zechariah and Daniel each reflect on its meaning.

insights.title: Millstones and lamplight
insights.body: God will take away the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp (25:10). Grinding grain each morning and lighting an oil lamp each evening were the most basic sounds and sights of a living household. Revelation uses the same pictures for Babylon's own fall.

insights.title: The cup of wrath
insights.body: Jeremiah is given a cup of the wine of wrath to make the nations drink (25:15). The image of judgment as a cup that makes people stagger runs through the prophets and into Revelation. Many readers connect it with the cup Jesus prayed might pass from him in Gethsemane.

insights.title: A code name for Babylon
insights.body: The king of Sheshach drinks last (25:26). Sheshach is Babylon written in a simple cipher, called atbash, which swaps the first letter of the alphabet for the last, the second for the second-last, and so on. Babylon, which hands the cup to others, must drink it too.

insights.title: A book within the book
insights.body: After all that is written in this book (25:13), the Greek Septuagint places the oracles against the nations, which the Hebrew text puts in chapters 46–51. The verse may once have introduced that collection. It is one of the clearest signs that Jeremiah circulated in two arrangements.

insights.title: Judgment begins at God's house
insights.body: Jerusalem drinks first (25:18). If God begins with the city called by his name, the nations cannot expect to be spared (25:29). Peter later says judgment begins with the household of God.

26.summary: At the start of Jehoiakim's reign Jeremiah predicts the temple will become like Shiloh, is put on trial for his life, and is saved when elders recall Micah's prophecy, though another prophet, Uriah, is killed.
26.lookfor: Watch who wants Jeremiah dead and who defends him, the precedent the elders cite, and the contrasting fate of Uriah.

names.name: Micah
names.gloss: The prophet from Moresheth who preached in Hezekiah's time, about a century earlier.

names.name: Uriah
names.gloss: A prophet from Kiriath Jearim who preached like Jeremiah and was executed.

names.name: Kiriath Jearim
names.gloss: A town west of Jerusalem where the ark once stayed.

names.name: Elnathan
names.gloss: A royal official sent to bring Uriah back from Egypt; he appears later pleading for Jeremiah's scroll.

names.name: Ahikam
names.gloss: Son of Shaphan, Josiah's scribe; he protects Jeremiah.

insights.title: The sermon's story
insights.body: This chapter tells what happened when Jeremiah preached the temple sermon recorded in chapter 7. Chapter 7 gives the message; chapter 26 gives the reaction. Placed here, it opens a section about how people responded to God's word.

insights.title: A trial at the New Gate
insights.body: Priests and prophets seize Jeremiah, and the royal officials come and sit at the entrance of the New Gate to hear the case (26:10). Gates were where courts met. The officials and people act as judges, while the priests and prophets act as accusers (26:11).

insights.title: Micah quoted
insights.body: Elders recall that Micah prophesied that Zion would be plowed as a field (26:18), and King Hezekiah repented instead of killing him. This is the only place in the prophets where one prophet's words are quoted with his name. It shows that prophetic sayings were remembered and treated as authoritative a century later.

insights.title: Uriah's different fate
insights.body: Uriah preached the same message, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim (26:20-23). Faithfulness did not guarantee survival. Elnathan, who fetched him, later urges the king not to burn Jeremiah's scroll.

insights.title: The family of Shaphan
insights.body: Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah (26:24). Shaphan was Josiah's scribe who read him the law book, and his family repeatedly supports Jeremiah. Ahikam's son Gedaliah became governor after the fall. A clay seal impression naming Gemariah son of Shaphan, Ahikam's brother, has been found in Jerusalem.

insights.title: Innocent blood
insights.body: Jeremiah warns that killing him would bring innocent blood on the city (26:15). Many have noted parallels with Jesus' trial: a prophet charged for predicting the temple's fall, accused by religious leaders before civil authorities. What do the differences in outcome highlight?

insights.title: God may relent
insights.body: God sends Jeremiah in hope that the people will turn and he may relent (26:3). Jeremiah repeats this at his trial (26:13). Judgment is announced in order to be averted, as the elders' example of Hezekiah shows (26:19).

27.summary: Jeremiah wears an ox yoke as a sign and tells the envoys of five neighboring kings, Zedekiah and the priests that all must serve Babylon and not listen to prophets promising a quick end.
27.lookfor: Watch the foreign envoys meeting in Jerusalem, God's claim to give the earth to whom he pleases, and what is said about the temple furnishings.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A wealthy Phoenician port city on the coast north of Israel.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: A Phoenician port city north of Tyre.

insights.title: Which king?
insights.body: The Hebrew text of 27:1 names Jehoiakim, but the chapter is about Zedekiah (27:3, 27:12), and 28:1 places it in his fourth year. A few Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read Zedekiah, and the Greek omits the verse. Most scholars think a copyist repeated the opening of 26:1.

insights.title: Bonds and bars
insights.body: Jeremiah makes bonds and bars (27:2), leather straps and wooden crossbars that joined an ox to its plough. Wearing them in public, he becomes a living sign of submission to Babylon. Breaking a yoke was a common image for freedom.

insights.title: A summit of rebels
insights.body: Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon come to Zedekiah (27:3), most likely to plan a revolt around 594 BC. Babylonian records mention unrest in Nebuchadnezzar's empire at about this time. Jeremiah sends each envoy home with a yoke and a warning.

insights.title: God gives kingdoms
insights.body: God made the earth and gives it to whom it seems right to me (27:5). The claim that Israel's God assigns empires among the nations is the foundation for the book of Daniel too. Babylon's power is on loan, until the time of his own land comes (27:7).

insights.title: Diviners and dreamers
insights.body: The nations have prophets, diviners, dream-interpreters, soothsayers and sorcerers (27:9). Ancient kings consulted many such experts before war, reading omens in animal livers, the stars or dreams. All of them were saying what kings wanted to hear.

insights.title: The pillars and the sea
insights.body: The bronze pillars, the bronze sea and the stands (27:19) were the great bronze works Solomon made for the temple. False prophets say the vessels already taken will soon return; Jeremiah says even these will go to Babylon. Yet God will bring them back in his time (27:22), as Ezra records.

insights.title: Submit and live
insights.body: Serve the king of Babylon, and live (27:17). Jeremiah calls for submission to a foreign oppressor as God's will for that moment. When is accepting a hard reality faithfulness, and when is it surrender to injustice?

28.summary: The prophet Hananiah publicly breaks Jeremiah's yoke and promises freedom within two years; Jeremiah answers that God will put an iron yoke in its place, and Hananiah dies that year.
28.lookfor: Watch how both men speak in the same way, Jeremiah's first reply, how he tests a prophet of peace, and the timing at the end.

names.name: Hananiah
names.gloss: A prophet from Gibeon who contradicts Jeremiah in the temple.

names.name: Gibeon
names.gloss: A town a few miles north-west of Jerusalem.

insights.title: Same words, opposite messages
insights.body: Hananiah opens with Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says (28:2), exactly as Jeremiah does. He also uses a sign-act, breaking the yoke. Onlookers had no outward way to tell which prophet was true.

insights.title: Amen, if only
insights.body: Jeremiah's first reply is Amen! May Yahweh do so (28:6). He genuinely wishes Hananiah were right. Why might the true prophet be the one who longs most to be proved wrong?

insights.title: Testing a prophet of peace
insights.body: Prophets of the past mostly announced war and disaster; a prophet of peace will be known when his word comes true (28:8-9). Jeremiah applies Deuteronomy's test: the burden of proof lies with the one promising comfort. Hananiah's two years (28:3) gave the test a deadline.

insights.title: Bars of iron
insights.body: Hananiah broke bars of wood, but in their place God makes bars of iron (28:13). The Hebrew word for the bars is motot, the crossbars of a yoke. Deuteronomy had warned of an iron yoke for a disobedient people.

insights.title: The fourth year of Zedekiah
insights.body: The scene is dated to the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year, about 594/593 BC (28:1), the same period as the envoys of chapter 27. Hope of revolt was in the air. Zedekiah also sent a mission to Babylon that year.

insights.title: Speaking rebellion
insights.body: Jeremiah says Hananiah will die because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh (28:16), the same phrase Deuteronomy uses of a false prophet. Hananiah dies two months later, in the seventh month (28:17). The narrator gives the date without comment.

insights.title: Hope too soon
insights.body: Hananiah promised everything back in two years; Jeremiah would promise return after seventy. The conflict is not between hope and doom but between cheap hope now and real hope later. The next chapter states Jeremiah's hope plainly.

29.summary: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon telling them to settle down, seek the city's welfare and wait seventy years for God's good plans, and he denounces false prophets among them.
29.lookfor: Watch the everyday instructions in the letter, the promise in 29:10-14 and its timing, and the angry letter from Babylon that answers Jeremiah.

names.name: Elasah
names.gloss: A son of Shaphan, brother of Ahikam, who carries the letter.

names.name: Gemariah
names.gloss: Son of Hilkiah, a royal envoy who also carries the letter.

names.name: Kolaiah
names.gloss: Father of Ahab, one of the false prophets in Babylon.

names.name: Shemaiah
names.gloss: A prophet among the exiles who writes to have Jeremiah silenced.

names.name: Nehelamite
names.gloss: A family or place name attached to Shemaiah, otherwise unknown.

names.name: Jehoiada
names.gloss: A famous priest of an earlier time who supervised the temple.

insights.title: Letters in Jeremiah's day
insights.body: The letter goes with envoys Zedekiah sent to Nebuchadnezzar (29:3). Letters on papyrus or pottery were common in this period; the Lachish ostraca, written by Judean officers shortly before Jerusalem fell, show the style. Shemaiah's reply from Babylon (29:25-28) shows letters travelling both ways.

insights.title: Build, plant, marry
insights.body: Build houses, plant gardens, marry and have children (29:5-6). These are the activities Deuteronomy names as part of settled life. The exiles are to put down roots in Babylon rather than wait for a quick return.

insights.title: The peace of the city
insights.body: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away, and pray for it (29:7). The word is shalom, wholeness and well-being. Praying for the enemy's capital was a radical instruction, and it shaped Jewish life in exile for centuries.

insights.title: Life in Babylonia
insights.body: Judean exiles lived in settlements such as Tel Abib by the Chebar canal.
