Cuneiform tablets from a Babylonian village called Al-Yahudu, the town of Judah, record Judean families buying, leasing and trading there over several generations. Many exiles did exactly what Jeremiah's letter advised.

insights.title: Plans for hope, in context
insights.body: God's thoughts of peace, to give you hope and a future (29:11) are among the most quoted words in the Bible. In context they come after seventy years (29:10) and are addressed to a community, not promising quick personal success. The promise to be found by those who seek with all their heart (29:13) echoes Deuteronomy.

insights.title: A roasted curse
insights.body: The false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah will be roasted in fire by the king of Babylon, and the exiles will use their names in a curse (29:22). The Hebrew plays on qalah, roast, and qelalah, curse. Babylonian burning as a punishment is also recalled in Daniel's furnace.

insights.title: The prophet in the stocks
insights.body: Shemaiah writes from Babylon urging the priest Zephaniah to put Jeremiah in the stocks as a madman (29:26-27). Zephaniah instead reads the letter to Jeremiah (29:29). The conflict over true prophecy stretched across hundreds of miles of desert.

insights.title: Seventy years again
insights.body: The seventy years of 25:11 appear again as the limit of exile (29:10). Daniel is pictured reading these words in Babylon near their end and praying for their fulfilment. Jeremiah's letter became a text later exiles read as addressed to them.

30.summary: God tells Jeremiah to write down promises that Israel and Judah will return, and that though their wound seems incurable he will heal them, break their yoke and raise up David their king.
30.lookfor: Watch the picture of men in labor pains, the swing between incurable wound and healing, and the ruler who is invited to draw near to God.

insights.title: The Book of Consolation
insights.body: Chapters 30–33 are often called the Book of Consolation, and God tells Jeremiah to write these words in a book (30:2). They gather Jeremiah's promises of restoration in one place, in the middle of the book's darkest narratives. The key phrase is reverse the captivity (30:3), a restoration of fortunes.

insights.title: Men in labor
insights.body: Jeremiah sees every man with his hands on his waist like a woman in labor (30:6). The grotesque image shows terror beyond normal experience. Childbirth pains are a frequent picture of panic in Jeremiah, but here they precede a deliverance (30:7).

insights.title: The time of Jacob's trouble
insights.body: That day is great, the time of Jacob's trouble, but he will be saved out of it (30:7). Historically it fits the fall of Jerusalem and exile. Some Christian traditions, especially dispensational ones, also read it of a future tribulation for Israel; most interpreters keep it in Jeremiah's own setting.

insights.title: David their king
insights.body: The freed people will serve Yahweh their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up (30:9). David had been dead four centuries, so this means a king from his line who rules as David did. Hosea and Ezekiel share the hope, which Jewish and Christian traditions read messianically.

insights.title: Incurable, then healed
insights.body: God says the wound is incurable and no medicine can help (30:12-13), and that he himself caused it (30:15). Then he says, I will restore health to you (30:17). What changes between these verses, if not Judah's condition?

insights.title: A city on its mound
insights.body: The city will be built on its own hill (30:18), literally its tel. Ancient cities were rebuilt on the ruins of earlier ones, slowly forming artificial mounds that archaeologists still excavate. Jerusalem's rebuilding is pictured on its old foundations.

insights.title: A ruler who approaches God
insights.body: The coming ruler will be one of their own, and God will bring him near; for who would dare to approach me? (30:21). Approaching God was a priestly privilege, and kings who presumed on it were punished. This ruler draws near by invitation, combining royal and priestly roles.

insights.title: The storm repeated
insights.body: The closing verses about the storm of Yahweh's wrath (30:23-24) repeat 23:19-20 almost word for word. There they were aimed at false prophets; here they fall on the wicked oppressors of God's people. In the latter days, God says, you will understand it.

31.summary: God promises to gather the scattered tribes with joy, comforts Rachel weeping for her children, and announces a new covenant in which his law will be written on his people's hearts.
31.lookfor: Watch the images of dancing and planting, Rachel's weeping and God's answer, Ephraim's repentance, and the four promises of the new covenant in 31:33-34.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: The capital of the former northern kingdom, whose hills will be replanted.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading northern tribe, standing for exiled Israel.

names.name: Ramah
names.gloss: A town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, near the traditional tomb of Rachel.

names.name: Rachel
names.gloss: Jacob's beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin and grandmother of Ephraim.

names.name: Hananel
names.gloss: A tower on the north wall of Jerusalem.

names.name: Gareb
names.gloss: An unidentified hill near Jerusalem.

names.name: Goah
names.gloss: An unidentified place near Jerusalem.

names.name: Kidron
names.gloss: The valley on Jerusalem's east side, between the city and the Mount of Olives.

insights.title: Everlasting love
insights.body: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness (31:3). Loving kindness translates hesed, God's faithful covenant love. The promise addresses the northern tribes, lost for over a century.

insights.title: Rachel weeping at Ramah
insights.body: Rachel, mother of the northern tribes, weeps from her grave for her lost children (31:15). One tradition placed her tomb near Ramah, in Benjamin. Ramah was also where the Babylonians gathered captives before deportation, as Jeremiah himself experienced.

insights.title: Rachel in Matthew
insights.body: Matthew quotes this verse after Herod's slaughter of Bethlehem's children. Another tradition placed Rachel's tomb near Bethlehem. Matthew links two moments of mothers' grief and, implicitly, the comfort that follows: in Jeremiah, God answers that her children will return (31:16-17).

insights.title: Turn me, and I will be turned
insights.body: Ephraim prays, Turn me, and I will be turned (31:18), using the root shuv once more. He recognizes that repentance itself is God's gift. God answers with a parent's yearning: my heart yearns for him (31:20).

insights.title: A woman encompasses a man
insights.body: Yahweh has created a new thing: a woman will encompass a man (31:22). The meaning is one of the hardest puzzles in Jeremiah. Interpretations include role reversal, Israel embracing God, and, among some early Christian writers, the virgin conceiving. What kind of new thing would the exiles have heard?

insights.title: Sour grapes
insights.body: The exiles quoted a proverb: the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge (31:29), meaning they suffered for their ancestors' sins. In the restored future each will die for his own sin (31:30). Ezekiel 18 takes up the same proverb at length.

insights.title: The new covenant
insights.body: God will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, writing his law on their hearts, so that all will know him and their sins will be forgiven (31:31-34). Jesus speaks of the new covenant in his blood at the Last Supper, and Hebrews quotes the passage in full, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New. Jewish interpreters read it as the renewal of the Torah within Israel; the Qumran community saw itself as a people of the new covenant.

insights.title: A valley made holy
insights.body: The rebuilt city will stretch from the tower of Hananel to the corner gate, and even the valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes will be holy to Yahweh (31:38-40). That valley is most likely Hinnom, the site of child sacrifice. The most defiled place becomes holy ground.

32.summary: During the final siege, imprisoned Jeremiah buys his cousin's field at Anathoth as a sign that land will again be bought in Judah, and prays as God reaffirms both judgment and restoration.
32.lookfor: Watch the legal steps of the purchase, where the deeds are stored and why, Jeremiah's prayer, and God's answer to his doubt.

names.name: Hanamel
names.gloss: Jeremiah's cousin, who offers to sell him the family field.

names.name: Shallum
names.gloss: Jeremiah's uncle, Hanamel's father.

names.name: Baruch
names.gloss: Jeremiah's scribe and companion, son of Neriah.

names.name: Molech
names.gloss: A god associated with child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom.

insights.title: A field under siege
insights.body: The tenth year of Zedekiah (32:1) is 588/587 BC, a year before the city fell. Babylonian troops held the countryside, including Anathoth. Jeremiah was confined in the court of the guard for predicting defeat (32:2-3), and land outside the walls was worthless.

insights.title: The right of redemption
insights.body: Hanamel says the right of redemption is yours (32:7). Israelite law gave the nearest relative the first right to buy land a family member had to sell, so it stayed in the clan. Ruth and Boaz's story turns on the same custom.

insights.title: A sealed deed and an open copy
insights.body: Jeremiah signs, seals and witnesses the deed, keeping one copy sealed and one open (32:10-11). This matches ancient practice: the full text was rolled and sealed, while a duplicate stayed readable for reference. Papyrus deeds of this double form have been found in Egypt and the Judean desert.

insights.title: Kept in a clay jar
insights.body: Baruch is told to put the deeds in an earthen vessel to last many days (32:14). Sealed jars protected documents from damp and pests, which is how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived for two thousand years. Clay seal impressions bearing the name of Berechiah son of Neriah the scribe have been published, but scholars dispute whether they are genuine.

insights.title: Seventeen shekels
insights.body: Jeremiah weighs out seventeen shekels of silver (32:9). Coins did not yet exist in Judah, so payment meant weighing silver on scales. A shekel was about 11 grams, so the price was around 190 grams of silver, though we cannot judge whether it was fair for a field under enemy occupation.

insights.title: Nothing too hard
insights.body: Jeremiah begins, There is nothing too hard for you (32:17), and God answers with the same words as a question (32:27). The phrase recalls God's question to Abraham about Sarah's son. Jeremiah's prayer ends with honest puzzlement about why he should buy land in a doomed city (32:25).

insights.title: An everlasting covenant
insights.body: God promises one heart and one way and an everlasting covenant, putting his fear in their hearts so they will not turn away (32:39-40). He will plant them with my whole heart and with my whole soul (32:41), the language Israel was commanded to love God with. Fields will again be bought and sealed (32:44).

33.summary: While Jeremiah is still imprisoned, God promises to heal the ruined city, restore the sounds of joy, raise up the righteous Branch of David and keep his covenants with David and the priests as surely as day and night.
33.lookfor: Watch the sounds that return to the empty streets, the new use of the name Yahweh our righteousness, and the covenant of day and night.

insights.title: Call to me
insights.body: Call to me, and I will answer you, and will show you great and difficult things (33:3). The verse is often read as a general promise about prayer. In context the hidden things are God's plans to restore a city whose houses are being torn down for defence (33:4).

insights.title: Houses torn down for walls
insights.body: The houses of Jerusalem and the royal palace were broken down to make a defence against the siege ramps (33:4). Defenders pulled down buildings near the walls for stone to thicken them. Isaiah describes the same in an earlier siege.

insights.title: The voices return
insights.body: The voices of bridegroom and bride, silenced in 7:34, 16:9 and 25:10, will be heard again (33:11). With them comes the temple song, Give thanks to Yahweh of Armies, for Yahweh is good, the refrain of Psalm 136. Ezra records this song at the laying of the second temple's foundation.

insights.title: Counting the flock
insights.body: Flocks will again pass under the hands of him who counts them (33:13). Shepherds counted sheep each evening as they entered the fold, often by touch with a staff. The detail paints a countryside safe and ordinary again.

insights.title: A name for the city
insights.body: Verses 33:15-16 repeat the promise of the righteous Branch from 23:5-6, with a twist. There the king was called Yahweh our righteousness; here the name belongs to Jerusalem. The city takes on the character of its king.

insights.title: Missing from the Greek
insights.body: The whole passage 33:14-26 is absent from the Greek Septuagint, the longest such gap in the book. Many scholars see it as a later expansion in the Hebrew edition; others think the Greek translators' source had lost it. Jewish and Christian Bibles that follow the Hebrew include it.

insights.title: David and the Levites
insights.body: David will never lack a man on his throne, nor the Levites a priest (33:17-18). After the exile there was no Davidic king, and the temple fell again in AD 70. Christians read this as fulfilled in Jesus as king and priest; Jewish tradition holds it as a promise awaiting fulfilment.

insights.title: As sure as day and night
insights.body: God's covenant with David is as unbreakable as his covenant of the day and night (33:20). As long as the sun rises, the promise stands. What does it mean to stake faith on the regularity of creation in an age when everything else has fallen?

34.summary: As Babylon besieges Judah's last cities, Jeremiah warns Zedekiah of capture, and condemns Jerusalem's leaders for freeing their Hebrew slaves under a solemn covenant and then taking them back.
34.lookfor: Watch the two cities still holding out, the ceremony of the cut calf, and the bitter wordplay on liberty in 34:17.

names.name: Lachish
names.gloss: Judah's second city, a fortress in the lowlands south-west of Jerusalem.

names.name: Azekah
names.gloss: A fortified town in the Shephelah, north of Lachish.

insights.title: Lachish and Azekah
insights.body: Only Lachish and Azekah remain among Judah's fortified cities (34:7). Among the Lachish letters, written on pottery by Judean officers in these last days, one reports that the writer is watching for the fire signals of Lachish because Azekah can no longer be seen. Many scholars think Azekah had just fallen.

insights.title: A peaceful death?
insights.body: Zedekiah is promised he will die in peace, with burnings like his fathers' (34:5). Royal funerals included burning spices, not cremation. Yet he was blinded and died a prisoner in Babylon. Some read the promise as conditional on his surrender; others note that he at least did not die by the sword (34:4).

insights.title: The law of release
insights.body: The law required Hebrew slaves, usually people sold for debt, to be freed after six years of service (34:14). God says Judah's ancestors ignored it. Under siege, Zedekiah's covenant to free them all (34:8-9) was a rare act of obedience.

insights.title: Freed, then re-enslaved
insights.body: The owners took their slaves back (34:11), most likely when the Babylonian army withdrew to face Egypt (34:21). Scholars suggest the release had practical motives as well: more defenders, fewer mouths to feed. When the danger seemed past, so did the promise.

insights.title: Liberty to the sword
insights.body: Liberty translates deror, the word for the jubilee release. Because they would not proclaim liberty, God proclaims to them a liberty to the sword, the pestilence and the famine (34:17). Isaiah and Jesus use the same word for the year of the Lord's favor.

insights.title: Walking between the pieces
insights.body: The leaders made their covenant by cutting a calf in two and walking between the halves (34:18-19). The rite meant: may I become like this animal if I break my oath. Ancient Near Eastern treaty texts describe similar rituals, and God himself passes between the pieces in his covenant with Abraham.

insights.title: Promises made in crisis
insights.body: The covenant was made in the temple, before God (34:15). When pressure lifted, it was broken. What does this episode say about vows made under threat, and about how God regards the treatment of the poor?

35.summary: Jeremiah tests the Rechabites by offering them wine in the temple, and their faithful refusal, in obedience to their ancestor, becomes a rebuke to Judah's disobedience to God.
35.lookfor: Watch the details of the Rechabites' way of life, why they are now in Jerusalem, and the promise they receive at the end.

names.name: Rechabites
names.gloss: A clan who kept a nomadic way of life in obedience to their ancestor Jonadab.

names.name: Jaazaniah
names.gloss: The Rechabite leader in Jeremiah's time, son of a different Jeremiah.

names.name: Jonadab
names.gloss: Son of Rechab, the clan's ancestor, who lived about 250 years earlier.

names.name: Hanan
names.gloss: A man of God whose sons had a room in the temple.

names.name: Maaseiah
names.gloss: A senior temple official, keeper of the threshold.

insights.title: Back in Jehoiakim's day
insights.body: The book steps back in time from Zedekiah to Jehoiakim (35:1). When Nebuchadnezzar invaded, and Aramean raiders came too, the tent-dwelling Rechabites took refuge in Jerusalem (35:11). Kings records these raiding bands at the end of Jehoiakim's reign.

insights.title: Jonadab son of Rechab
insights.body: Jonadab rode with Jehu in his violent purge of Baal worship around 841 BC. Chronicles may link the Rechabites to the Kenites. His descendants had kept his rules for some two and a half centuries.

insights.title: No wine, no houses, no fields
insights.body: The Rechabites drink no wine, build no houses, sow no fields and plant no vineyards (35:6-7). This was a deliberate rejection of settled farming life, perhaps seen as the way to Canaanite religion. Their vow resembles a Nazirite's in part but was lifelong and for a whole clan.

insights.title: Rooms in the temple
insights.body: Jeremiah brings them into a named room near the officials' chamber and above that of Maaseiah, keeper of the threshold (35:4). The temple courts had many side rooms used by priests, officials and guilds. The precise directions suggest an eyewitness account.

insights.title: A test not meant to be passed
insights.body: God tells Jeremiah to set wine before them (35:5), knowing they will refuse. The point is not to tempt them but to stage a public contrast. A family keeps a human ancestor's rule for centuries; God's people will not keep his commands though he sent prophets early and often (35:14-15).

insights.title: Rising up early
insights.body: I have spoken to you, rising up early and speaking (35:14) is a phrase used about a dozen times in Jeremiah. It pictures God as someone who gets up early to begin urgent work. It stresses how persistently God spoke.

insights.title: A man to stand before me
insights.body: Jonadab will not lack a man to stand before me forever (35:19). The wording echoes the promises to David and to the priests in chapter 33. To stand before God is the language of a servant or priest. Faithfulness from an outsider clan is honored with a lasting place.

36.summary: Jeremiah dictates his prophecies to Baruch, who reads them in the temple; the scroll reaches King Jehoiakim, who cuts it up and burns it piece by piece, and Jeremiah dictates it again with more added.
36.lookfor: Watch the scroll's journey from the people to the officials to the king, how each group reacts, and what the officials do with the scroll before going to the king.

names.name: Baruch
names.gloss: Son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe and companion.

names.name: Gemariah
names.gloss: Son of Shaphan, an official from whose room the scroll is read.

names.name: Micaiah
names.gloss: Gemariah's son, who reports the reading to the officials.

names.name: Elishama
names.gloss: The royal scribe or secretary.

names.name: Delaiah
names.gloss: An official who pleads with the king not to burn the scroll.

names.name: Jehudi
names.gloss: A court official who reads the scroll to the king.

names.name: Jerahmeel
names.gloss: A royal prince sent to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah.

insights.title: The fourth and fifth years of Jehoiakim
insights.body: The scroll is written in 605 BC, the year of Carchemish (36:1), and read on a fast day in the ninth month of the next year (36:9), December 604. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar sacked Ashkelon at about that time. A public fast in such danger gave the scroll a large and anxious audience.

insights.title: Ink and columns
insights.body: Baruch writes with ink on a scroll (36:18), most likely papyrus or leather. The leaves Jehudi reads (36:23) are columns of text. The king cuts each section off with a scribe's knife, a tool normally used to trim reed pens and scrolls.

insights.title: Josiah tore, Jehoiakim cut
insights.body: When Josiah heard the law book read, he tore his clothes and sought God. When Jehoiakim hears Jeremiah's scroll, he cuts it, and no one tears their garments (36:24). The Hebrew uses the same verb, qara, for the king cutting the scroll and the garments not being torn, a sharp contrast between father and son.

insights.title: Names in clay
insights.body: A clay seal impression reading Gemariah son of Shaphan was excavated in the City of David, in a layer from the Babylonian destruction. Other seal impressions naming people in this chapter, such as Jerahmeel the king's son and Baruch the scribe, have appeared on the antiquities market and are of disputed authenticity. They show at least how common such official seals were.

insights.title: The winter house
insights.body: The king sits in his winter house before a brazier (36:22). Wealthy households had rooms or wings built to be warm in the cold, rainy Jerusalem winter. The domestic detail heightens the scene: the word of God is fed to a heater.

insights.title: The officials' divided response
insights.body: The officials are afraid, tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide, and plead with the king, yet they go along with the reading (36:16-25). What would faithfulness have required of them?

insights.title: A book that grew
insights.body: The second scroll contains all the words of the first, and many similar words were added (36:32). This is a rare biblical account of how a prophetic book was written and expanded. It supports the view that Jeremiah's book developed in stages, and that a king could burn the scroll but not the word.

37.summary: When Egypt's army briefly draws Babylon away, Jeremiah warns Zedekiah that the siege will return, is arrested as a deserter while leaving the city, and is thrown into a dungeon before the king secretly consults him.
37.lookfor: Watch Zedekiah's repeated requests, why Jeremiah leaves the city, and the question the king asks in secret.

names.name: Jehucal
names.gloss: An official sent by the king, son of Shelemiah.

names.name: Irijah
names.gloss: The captain at the Benjamin gate who arrests Jeremiah.

names.name: Jonathan
names.gloss: A royal scribe whose house had been made into a prison.

insights.title: Egypt to the rescue?
insights.body: Pharaoh's army marched out of Egypt and the Babylonians lifted the siege to meet it (37:5). The pharaoh was probably Hophra, named in 44:30. Jerusalem's leaders hoped for deliverance, but Jeremiah said Egypt would turn back and Babylon return (37:7-8).

insights.title: Even if only wounded men remained
insights.body: Even if Judah defeated the whole Babylonian army and only wounded men were left, they would rise and burn the city (37:10). The exaggeration makes the point that the issue is not military strength but God's decision.

insights.title: Receiving his portion
insights.body: During the lull Jeremiah heads to Benjamin to receive his portion there (37:12). The phrase probably refers to a share of family property, perhaps connected with the field he later buys from his cousin. Leaving through the Benjamin gate toward the enemy's lines looked like desertion.

insights.title: A prophet accused of treason
insights.body: Irijah charges Jeremiah with defecting to the Chaldeans (37:13). Since Jeremiah had urged surrender, the accusation was plausible. Amos too was accused of conspiracy against the king, and Jesus was charged with subverting the nation.

insights.title: A house turned prison
insights.body: Jeremiah is held in the house of Jonathan the scribe, which had been made into a prison, in a dungeon house with cells (37:15-16). Israel's law had no long-term prisons; captives were held in pits, cisterns or rooms until a decision. The conditions were bad enough that Jeremiah feared he would die there (37:20).

insights.title: Is there any word?
insights.body: Zedekiah asks secretly, Is there any word from Yahweh? and Jeremiah answers, There is: you will be handed to the king of Babylon (37:17). The king wants to hear but cannot act on what he hears. Why does he keep asking?

insights.title: Bread while it lasted
insights.body: Moved to the court of the guard, Jeremiah receives a loaf a day from the bakers' street until all the bread in the city was gone (37:21). The detail of a street of bakers shows that crafts clustered by trade. It also quietly marks the growing famine.

38.summary: Officials have Jeremiah lowered into a muddy cistern to die, an Ethiopian court official rescues him, and Zedekiah again consults him secretly but cannot bring himself to surrender.
38.lookfor: Watch the officials' charge against Jeremiah, the care of his rescuer, the king's fears, and the image of sinking in mud that returns at the end.

names.name: Shephatiah
names.gloss: An official, son of Mattan, who demands Jeremiah's death.

names.name: Gedaliah
names.gloss: Gedaliah son of Pashhur, an official, not the later governor.

names.name: Jucal
names.gloss: Another form of Jehucal, an official, son of Shelemiah.

names.name: Malchijah
names.gloss: A royal prince who owned the cistern.

names.name: Ebedmelech
names.gloss: An Ethiopian eunuch in the palace, whose name means servant of the king.

insights.title: Seals of Jeremiah's enemies
insights.body: Excavations in the City of David have found clay seal impressions naming Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur, matching two officials here (38:1). Most archaeologists accept the identification, though some urge caution since the names were not rare. They are among the closest archaeological links to people in the Bible.

insights.title: Weakening the hands
insights.body: The officials say Jeremiah weakens the hands of the soldiers (38:4), a Hebrew idiom for demoralizing. One of the Lachish letters from these same months complains about officials' words that weaken the hands of the land. The phrase was part of the political vocabulary of the siege.

insights.title: A king who cannot say no
insights.body: Zedekiah tells the officials, Behold, he is in your hand; for the king can't do anything to oppose you (38:5). He then lets Ebedmelech rescue Jeremiah (38:10) and swears in secret to protect him (38:16). The portrait is of a ruler pulled every way and decided in none.

insights.title: A cistern of mud
insights.body: Jeremiah is lowered into a cistern with no water but mud, and sinks into it (38:6). Plastered cisterns stored rainwater, and by late in a siege they could be nearly dry. Joseph was thrown into a dry pit, and Psalm 40 praises God for lifting the psalmist out of the miry clay.

insights.title: The Ethiopian who acted
insights.body: Ebedmelech, a Cushite from the upper Nile region, confronts the king and lifts Jeremiah out (38:7-13). He even sends rags to pad the ropes under Jeremiah's arms (38:12). A foreigner and court servant does what Judah's officials would not, and he receives his own promise in the next chapter.

insights.title: Feet sunk in the mire
insights.body: Jeremiah warns that the palace women will taunt Zedekiah: your feet are sunk in the mire, and your friends have turned away (38:22). Jeremiah had just been literally stuck in mud. The king who let him sink will find himself sinking.

insights.title: Half the truth
insights.body: At the king's request Jeremiah tells the officials only part of the conversation (38:24-27). The narrator neither praises nor condemns him. Readers have long debated whether withholding truth to save a life is ever right; the Hebrew midwives and Samuel offer other examples.

39.summary: After an eighteen-month siege Jerusalem falls; Zedekiah is captured, made to watch his sons' execution and blinded, the city is burned, and Jeremiah is released and placed with Gedaliah, while Ebedmelech is promised his life.
39.lookfor: Watch the dates, the names of the Babylonian officials, Zedekiah's attempted escape, and who is spared and why.

names.name: Nergal Sharezer
names.gloss: A Babylonian official, probably the Neriglissar who later became king of Babylon.

names.name: Sarsechim
names.gloss: A Babylonian official, probably chief of the court officials.

names.name: Riblah
names.gloss: Nebuchadnezzar's military headquarters in Syria, on the Orontes river.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A region of central Syria.

names.name: Nebuzaradan
names.gloss: Commander of Nebuchadnezzar's guard, who carried out the destruction of Jerusalem.

names.name: Nebushazban
names.gloss: A Babylonian official, chief of the court officials.

names.name: Gedaliah
names.gloss: Son of Ahikam, appointed governor of Judah by Babylon.

names.name: Ebedmelech
names.gloss: The Ethiopian official who rescued Jeremiah from the cistern.

insights.title: The dates of the fall
insights.body: The siege began in the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, January 588 BC, and the wall was breached in the fourth month of his eleventh year, summer 587 or 586 BC (39:1-2). Scholars still debate which of the two years is correct. After the exile Jews kept fasts in the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months, which Jewish tradition links with these events.

insights.title: Babylonian officials by name
insights.body: The officials who sit in the middle gate (39:3) include titles as well as names: Rabsaris means chief official and Rabmag is another high rank. Nergal Sharezer is probably Neriglissar, who became king in 560 BC. A Babylonian tablet in the British Museum names a chief official, Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, whom many scholars identify with Sarsechim.

insights.title: The escape by night
insights.body: Zedekiah and his soldiers flee by the king's garden through the gate between the two walls, heading for the Arabah, the Jordan valley (39:4). The route led out of the south end of the city near the pool of Siloam. Ezekiel had acted out a king slipping out through a hole in the wall at night.

insights.title: He will not see it
insights.body: Zedekiah sees his sons killed, and then his eyes are put out (39:6-7). Jeremiah had said he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye. Ezekiel had said he would be brought to Babylon but would not see it. Both came true.

insights.title: Land for the poor
insights.body: Nebuzaradan leaves the poorest people in Judah and gives them vineyards and fields (39:10). The very people the rich had re-enslaved in chapter 34 now receive the land. Babylon's policy was practical, keeping the land farmed, but the reversal is striking.

insights.title: Two accounts of release
insights.body: Here Jeremiah is taken from the court of the guard and handed to Gedaliah (39:14). In 40:1 he is released from chains at Ramah, among the captives. Some see two stages of one event, Jeremiah swept up in the general round-up after first being freed; others see two traditions placed side by side. The Greek text also lacks 39:4-13.

insights.title: Because you trusted me
insights.body: The chapter ends by stepping back to the promise given to Ebedmelech while Jeremiah was still confined (39:15-18). He will escape with his life because you have put your trust in me (39:18). Amid the city's ruin, a foreigner's faith is singled out.

40.summary: Freed by Nebuzaradan, Jeremiah chooses to stay with the new governor Gedaliah at Mizpah, where scattered Judeans gather and harvest, but Gedaliah refuses to believe a warning of a plot against his life.
40.lookfor: Watch the Babylonian commander's speech, the brief recovery under Gedaliah, and the warning he dismisses.

names.name: Ramah
names.gloss: A town north of Jerusalem where captives were gathered for deportation.

names.name: Mizpah
names.gloss: A town about eight miles north of Jerusalem that became Gedaliah's seat of government.

names.name: Ishmael
names.gloss: Son of Nethaniah, an officer of the royal family.

names.name: Johanan
names.gloss: Son of Kareah, a leading army officer who survived the fall.

names.name: Netophathite
names.gloss: Someone from Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.

names.name: Jezaniah
names.gloss: An army officer, son of the Maacathite.

names.name: Baalis
names.gloss: King of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan.

insights.title: A pagan officer's sermon
insights.body: Nebuzaradan tells Jeremiah that Yahweh your God pronounced this evil and brought it because the people sinned (40:2-3). The Babylonian sounds like a prophet. The book lets an outsider state its own explanation of the disaster, as Deuteronomy said the nations would.

insights.title: Mizpah under Babylon
insights.body: With Jerusalem in ruins, Gedaliah governs from Mizpah (40:6), usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh north of Jerusalem. Excavations there show the town continued to flourish in the Babylonian period. A seal found there reading Jaazaniah servant of the king may belong to the officer named in 40:8.

insights.title: Baalis king of Ammon
insights.body: A seal impression found in Jordan names Baalyasha king of the Ammonites, widely taken to be the Baalis of 40:14. Ammon had joined the plots against Babylon, and a pro-Babylonian governor in Judah was a threat to it. It later shelters the assassin (41:15).

insights.title: Gedaliah's family
insights.body: Gedaliah is the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan (40:5), the family that had protected Jeremiah. His appointment fit Jeremiah's message to accept Babylon's rule. His advice, Serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you (40:9), echoes Jeremiah's own.

insights.title: A harvest after the fall
insights.body: Jews return from Moab, Ammon and Edom and gather very much wine and summer fruits (40:12). After the siege, an abundant harvest suggests God's promise that life would go on in the land. For a few months the remnant seems to have a future.

insights.title: Trusting too well
insights.body: Gedaliah refuses to believe Johanan's warning and forbids him to kill Ishmael (40:14-16). Was his refusal admirable integrity or fatal naivety? The next chapter gives the cost.

insights.title: The remnant gathers
insights.body: The scattered of Judah gather back to the land (40:11-12) in a small foretaste of the return the prophets promised. The episode shows how fragile that hope was when left to human leaders.

41.summary: Ishmael murders Gedaliah at a meal, slaughters pilgrims and takes captives toward Ammon, until Johanan rescues the captives, who then prepare to flee to Egypt in fear of Babylon.
41.lookfor: Watch the betrayal at the shared meal, the pilgrims from the north and what they carry, and the old cistern that becomes a mass grave.

names.name: Ishmael
names.gloss: Son of Nethaniah, of the royal family, who assassinates Gedaliah.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: An ancient city in the central hills of the former northern kingdom.

names.name: Shiloh
names.gloss: The old sanctuary town north of Jerusalem.

names.name: Asa
names.gloss: A king of Judah about three centuries earlier.

names.name: Baasha
names.gloss: A king of the northern kingdom who fought Asa.

names.name: Gibeon
names.gloss: A town near Mizpah with a large pool.

names.name: Geruth Chimham
names.gloss: A lodging place near Bethlehem, probably named after Chimham, a friend of David.

insights.title: A royal grudge
insights.body: Ishmael is of the royal offspring (41:1). As a member of David's family he may have resented a non-royal governor serving Babylon, and he had Ammon's backing (40:14). Killing Gedaliah also meant killing the Babylonian soldiers stationed with him (41:3).

insights.title: Murder at the table
insights.body: They ate bread together in Mizpah (41:1) before Ishmael struck. Sharing a meal created a bond of trust and hospitality. Breaking it with murder was a deep betrayal, a theme Psalms 41 and 55 lament.

insights.title: The Fast of Gedaliah
insights.body: Gedaliah was killed in the seventh month (41:1). Jewish tradition keeps a fast day after the New Year, the Fast of Gedaliah, linked with the fast of the seventh month mentioned in Zechariah. His death ended the last Judean self-government after the fall.

insights.title: Pilgrims to a ruined temple
insights.body: Eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria come in mourning, with shaved beards and cut bodies, carrying offerings for Yahweh's house (41:5). Worship continued at the site of the destroyed temple. These northerners show that faith had survived in the old kingdom of Israel.

insights.title: Asa's cistern
insights.body: Ishmael throws the bodies into the cistern that King Asa had made when fortifying Mizpah against Baasha (41:9). A defensive work built by a king of Judah becomes a mass grave dug by a prince of Judah.

insights.title: The pool of Gibeon
insights.body: Johanan catches Ishmael by the great waters of Gibeon (41:12). Archaeologists at el-Jib uncovered a huge rock-cut pool with a spiral stair descending to the water table. It was the site of an earlier clash between David's and Saul's men.

insights.title: Back toward Egypt
insights.body: The rescued remnant stops near Bethlehem on the way to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (41:17-18). Babylon was likely to punish the murder of its governor on whoever remained. The road to Egypt reverses the exodus, which the law had warned against.

42.summary: The remnant asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance and promises to obey; after ten days God says to stay in Judah and not fear Babylon, but Jeremiah perceives they have already decided to go to Egypt.
42.lookfor: Watch the people's solemn promise, the wait before God answers, the attractions of Egypt, and how the promises echo Jeremiah's call.

names.name: Johanan
names.gloss: The army officer now leading the remnant.

names.name: Jezaniah
names.gloss: An officer, son of Hoshaiah, perhaps the same as Azariah in 43:2.

insights.title: A promise to obey either way
insights.body: The people swear to obey whether it is good or bad (42:6), calling God as witness against themselves (42:5). Israel had promised the same at Sinai. Their words will be tested within days.

insights.title: Ten days of waiting
insights.body: God's word comes after ten days (42:7). Jeremiah could not produce a word on demand, which marks him off from prophets who answered instantly. The wait also tested the people's patience under danger.

insights.title: I grieve over the distress
insights.body: God says, I grieve over the distress that I have brought on you (42:10). The verb, naham, can mean to relent, regret or be comforted. Judgment was real, but God takes no pleasure in it.

insights.title: Build, plant, do not fear
insights.body: If they stay, God will build and not pull down, plant and not uproot (42:10), and he is with them to save (42:11). The words of Jeremiah's call come back. The hopeful half of his commission is offered to the remnant in Judah.

insights.title: No war, no trumpet, no hunger
insights.body: Egypt seemed a land where we will see no war, nor hear the trumpet, nor be hungry (42:14). It was a rich, stable country with a long tradition of welcoming refugees, and Judean soldiers had served there. Like the Israelites in the wilderness who missed Egypt's food, the remnant looked back for security.

insights.title: Asking for guidance already decided
insights.body: Jeremiah tells them they have deceived themselves: they asked for God's word but never meant to obey (42:20-21). How often do people seek guidance hoping only for confirmation?

insights.title: No going back to Egypt
insights.body: Don't go into Egypt! (42:19). The law forbade the king to lead the people back to Egypt, and Isaiah warned against relying on its horses. Going down to Egypt would undo the exodus in a single journey.

43.summary: The leaders reject Jeremiah's word as a lie and take the remnant, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, to Egypt; at Tahpanhes Jeremiah buries stones and announces that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne there.
43.lookfor: Watch who the leaders blame, who is taken to Egypt, and the sign-act Jeremiah performs at Pharaoh's building.

names.name: Azariah
names.gloss: Son of Hoshaiah, an officer who calls Jeremiah a liar.

names.name: Baruch
names.gloss: Jeremiah's scribe, accused of turning him against the people.

names.name: Tahpanhes
names.gloss: An Egyptian frontier fortress on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta.

names.name: Beth Shemesh
names.gloss: Here an Egyptian city, Heliopolis, known for its obelisks; the name means house of the sun.

insights.title: Blaming Baruch
insights.body: The leaders say Yahweh did not send Jeremiah; Baruch has turned you against us (43:3). They cannot reject the old prophet openly, so they blame his scribe. It shows how influential Baruch had become.

insights.title: Taken against his will
insights.body: Jeremiah had chosen to stay in the land. Now he and Baruch are taken with the remnant to Egypt (43:6). The prophet who called for staying ends his life in the place he warned against. Scripture never records his death; a later Jewish tradition says he was stoned in Egypt.

insights.title: The brick pavement at Tahpanhes
insights.body: Tahpanhes was the Greek Daphnae, at modern Tell Defenneh. In the 1880s Flinders Petrie excavated a fort there with a large brick platform in front of it, which locals called the palace of the Jew's daughter. Petrie linked it with the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh's house (43:9), though this is not certain.

insights.title: Babylon reaches Egypt
insights.body: Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne over the hidden stones (43:10). A fragmentary Babylonian text records a campaign against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568 BC. It did not conquer Egypt, but it showed that fleeing there was no escape.

insights.title: Beth Shemesh in Egypt
insights.body: Beth Shemesh means house of the sun (43:13). Here it translates the Egyptian city of On, called Heliopolis by the Greeks, centre of the sun god's worship. Its pillars are obelisks; one still stands at the site, and others now stand in Rome, London and New York.

insights.title: Wrapping like a shepherd
insights.body: He will array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd puts on his garment (43:12). Some translators read the verb as picking clean, as a shepherd picks his cloak free of lice. Either way, Egypt will be taken over with ease.

insights.title: The exodus in reverse
insights.body: They came into the land of Egypt (43:7). Israel's story began with escape from Egypt; the remnant of Judah now walks back into it. The prophets used return to Egypt as a picture of undoing the covenant, and here it happens in history.

44.summary: Jeremiah confronts the Judeans living across Egypt for worshipping other gods, and they answer that life was better when they burned incense to the queen of the sky; Jeremiah announces judgment and a sign concerning Pharaoh Hophra.
44.lookfor: Watch the places where Judeans now live, the people's explanation of their disaster, the role the women and their husbands play, and the sign at the end.

names.name: Migdol
names.gloss: A fortress town on Egypt's north-eastern frontier.

names.name: Tahpanhes
names.gloss: An Egyptian frontier fortress in the eastern Nile Delta.

names.name: Memphis
names.gloss: The ancient capital of Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo.

names.name: Pathros
names.gloss: Upper, or southern, Egypt.

names.name: Hophra
names.gloss: Pharaoh of Egypt from 589 to 570 BC, known to the Greeks as Apries.

insights.title: Judeans across Egypt
insights.body: Judeans already live in the north at Migdol, Tahpanhes and Memphis, and far south in Pathros (44:1). A century later, papyri from Elephantine, an island on the Nile in the far south, show a Jewish military colony there with its own temple to Yahu. Some of those documents also mention other deities alongside him, much as this chapter describes.

insights.title: Two readings of history
insights.body: The people say that when they worshipped the queen of the sky they had plenty, and since they stopped they have lacked everything (44:17-18). They probably meant the time since Josiah's reform. Jeremiah reads the same events the opposite way (44:21-23). How do people decide which story explains their suffering?

insights.title: The queen of the sky
insights.body: The goddess called the queen of the sky was most likely Ishtar or Astarte, honored with incense, drink offerings and cakes, perhaps shaped in her image (44:19). Her worship was especially popular with women and households. Jeremiah had already condemned it in Jerusalem.

insights.title: Wives, husbands and vows
insights.body: The women ask whether they made offerings without our husbands (44:19). Under Israel's law a husband could approve or cancel his wife's vows. The women's point is that the whole family shared the practice, so the men cannot blame them alone.

insights.title: Keep your vows, then
insights.body: Jeremiah answers with grim irony: establish then your vows, and perform your vows (44:25). Since they insist, God will let them have their way. Then he swears that his name will no longer be on the lips of Judeans in Egypt (44:26).

insights.title: Whose word will stand
insights.body: The remnant will know whose word will stand, mine or theirs (44:28). The whole chapter is a contest between the people's vow and God's word. A small remnant will still escape back to Judah, so even here judgment is not total (44:28).

insights.title: The end of Hophra
insights.body: The sign is that Pharaoh Hophra will be handed over to his enemies, as Zedekiah was (44:30). The Greek historian Herodotus records that Hophra, whom he calls Apries, was overthrown in a revolt led by his general Amasis and later killed. The Egyptian king Judah trusted proved no safer than its own.

45.summary: In a short word dated years earlier, God answers Baruch's weariness and ambition, telling him not to seek great things in a time of ruin but promising him his life.
45.lookfor: Watch the date, Baruch's complaint, and the one thing God promises him.

names.name: Baruch
names.gloss: Son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe and faithful companion.

insights.title: A message out of order
insights.body: The oracle is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605 BC, when Baruch wrote the scroll (45:1). It is placed here, after the story of the flight to Egypt, as a kind of signature at the end of the narratives about Jeremiah. In the Greek Septuagint it comes at the very end of the book.

insights.title: Baruch's lament
insights.body: Baruch says, Woe is me now! I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest (45:3). His complaint sounds like Jeremiah's own confessions. Writing down years of judgment oracles, and risking arrest for them, had cost him too.

insights.title: God's own loss
insights.body: God answers that he himself is breaking down what he built and uprooting what he planted (45:4). The verbs of Jeremiah's call return. Baruch's pain is set within God's greater grief over his own work.

insights.title: A scribal family
insights.body: Baruch's brother Seraiah served as a royal quartermaster, and their grandfather Mahseiah is named in 32:12. Baruch may have come from a prominent family with prospects at court. That may be the background to God's question, Do you seek great things for yourself? (45:5).

insights.title: Your life as a prize
insights.body: God says, I will let you escape with your life (45:5). The Hebrew is literally I will give you your life as booty, a prize of war. The same phrase is used for those who surrender and for Ebedmelech. In a time of total loss, survival itself is the gift.

insights.title: Not great things
insights.body: Don't seek great things for yourself (45:5). Baruch is asked to accept a faithful, unnoticed life while the world collapses around him. What might such a word mean for ambition in the service of God?

insights.title: Baruch's later fame
insights.body: The book that bears Jeremiah's name owes much to Baruch. Later Jewish writers produced several works in his name, and the Book of Baruch is part of Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, though not in Jewish or Protestant Bibles. The man told not to seek great things became one of the best-remembered scribes of the Bible.

46.summary: The oracles against the nations begin with Egypt, mocking its army's defeat by Babylon at Carchemish and foretelling Nebuchadnezzar's invasion, before ending with a promise to Jacob.
46.lookfor: Watch the vivid battle orders and the sudden rout, the images of the Nile and the heifer, and the promise to Israel at the end.

names.name: Necoh
names.gloss: Pharaoh Neco II of Egypt (610–595 BC), who killed Josiah.

names.name: Carchemish
names.gloss: A city on the upper Euphrates, scene of a decisive battle in 605 BC.

names.name: Cush
names.gloss: The kingdom south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan, supplying soldiers.

names.name: Put
names.gloss: Probably Libya, west of Egypt, supplying soldiers.

names.name: Ludim
names.gloss: Archers serving in Egypt's army, perhaps from Lydia in Asia Minor.

names.name: Migdol
names.gloss: A fortress on Egypt's north-eastern border.

names.name: Amon
names.gloss: Amun, chief god of Thebes and Egypt's state religion.

names.name: No
names.gloss: Thebes, the great city of Upper Egypt.

insights.title: Oracles against the nations
insights.body: Chapters 46–51 gather Jeremiah's oracles against foreign nations, a form found in most of the prophets. They fulfil his call as a prophet to the nations (1:5) and show that Israel's God rules the whole world. The order begins with Egypt and climbs to Babylon.

insights.title: The battle of Carchemish
insights.body: In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, still crown prince, crushed Necoh's Egyptian army at Carchemish (46:2). The Babylonian Chronicle records the victory and the pursuit of the Egyptians. It ended Egypt's control of Syria and Judah and opened the way for Babylon.

insights.title: Rising like the Nile
insights.body: Egypt rises up like the Nile, boasting it will cover the earth (46:7-8). Each summer the Nile flooded and covered the valley, bringing Egypt its wealth. Jeremiah turns the national symbol into an image of arrogant ambition.

insights.title: Why has Apis fled?
insights.body: The Hebrew of 46:15, Why are your strong ones swept away? can also be divided to read, Why has Apis fled? The Greek Septuagint takes it that way. Apis was the sacred bull of Memphis, and the beautiful heifer of 46:20 may play on the same cult.

insights.title: A big noise
insights.body: The soldiers call Pharaoh but a noise; he has let the appointed time pass by (46:17). It sounds like a mocking nickname, perhaps Big Noise who missed his chance. Isaiah gave Egypt a similar name, Rahab who sits still.

insights.title: Balm in vain
insights.body: Egypt is told to go to Gilead for balm, but no medicine will heal her (46:11). Jeremiah used the same picture for Judah. Egypt, famed for its physicians, has no cure for what God has decreed.

insights.title: Egypt will be inhabited again
insights.body: After the judgment, Egypt will be inhabited as in the days of old (46:26). Like Moab, Ammon and Elam later, Egypt receives a word of future restoration. The oracles against the nations are not only about destruction.

insights.title: Don't be afraid, Jacob
insights.body: The chapter ends with words to Israel repeated from 30:10-11 (46:27-28). God will make a full end of the nations where Israel is scattered, but not of Israel. The judgment on Egypt is set beside the hope for God's people.

47.summary: A flood from the north will sweep over the Philistines, so terrifying that fathers flee without their children, and the sword of Yahweh will not rest until its task is done.
47.lookfor: Watch the sound of the approaching army, the effect on the fathers, and the dialogue with the sword at the end.

names.name: Philistines
names.gloss: The people of the southern coastal plain, long Israel's rivals.

names.name: Gaza
names.gloss: The southernmost Philistine city.

names.name: Caphtor
names.gloss: Probably Crete, remembered as the Philistines' place of origin.

names.name: Ashkelon
names.gloss: A Philistine seaport north of Gaza.

insights.title: When Pharaoh struck Gaza
insights.body: The oracle is dated before Pharaoh struck Gaza (47:1). The event is uncertain; Necoh's campaigns around 609 BC or later actions are both possible. The flood comes from the north, which points to Babylon.

insights.title: Ashkelon destroyed
insights.body: The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in late 604 BC. Excavations at Ashkelon have uncovered a destruction layer from that time, with burned buildings and victims. Gaza and Ashkelon are both named in this oracle (47:5).

insights.title: Fathers who don't look back
insights.body: At the thunder of hoofs and chariot wheels, the fathers don't look back to their children (47:3). Terror overcomes even the instinct to protect one's children. The detail captures the panic of a city under sudden attack.

insights.title: From Caphtor
insights.body: The Philistines are called the remnant of the isle of Caphtor (47:4). Amos says God brought the Philistines from Caphtor as he brought Israel from Egypt. Most scholars think the Philistines were among the Sea Peoples who came from the Aegean region around 1200 BC.

insights.title: Baldness and cutting
insights.body: Baldness has come on Gaza, and Ashkelon is asked, how long will you cut yourself? (47:5). Shaving the head and cutting the skin were mourning rituals. The cities are pictured as mourners.

insights.title: Sword, be still
insights.body: Someone cries to the sword of Yahweh to return to its sheath and rest (47:6), but the answer comes: how can it rest, when Yahweh has commanded it? (47:7). Is the first voice the Philistines, the prophet, or anyone weary of war?

insights.title: Even old enemies
insights.body: The Philistines were Israel's enemies from the days of Samson and David. Here they are not judged for what they did to Israel but simply fall under the same northern flood. Zechariah later pictures a remnant of Philistines joining God's people.

48.summary: A long lament over Moab announces its destruction for pride and trust in Chemosh, naming town after town, yet ends with a promise that God will restore Moab's fortunes.
48.lookfor: Watch for Moab's pride and complacency, the image of wine left on its lees, God's own weeping, and the last verse.

names.name: Nebo
names.gloss: A Moabite town near the mountain from which Moses saw the promised land.

names.name: Heshbon
names.gloss: A city on the plateau east of the Jordan, once the Amorite king Sihon's capital.

names.name: Chemosh
names.gloss: The national god of Moab.

names.name: Dibon
names.gloss: A major Moabite city, where the Moabite Stone was found.

names.name: Aroer
names.gloss: A town on the north rim of the Arnon gorge.

names.name: Arnon
names.gloss: A deep gorge cutting through Moab to the Dead Sea.

names.name: Kerioth
names.gloss: A Moabite city with a temple of Chemosh.

names.name: Kir Heres
names.gloss: A fortress city of Moab, probably modern Kerak.

skim.advice: The many place names in 48:1-5, 48:18-24 and 48:31-34 can be read quickly; read closely the verses on Moab's complacency, God's mourning and the final promise.

insights.title: The Moabite Stone
insights.body: The Moabite Stone, set up by King Mesha around 840 BC and found at Dibon in 1868, is the longest inscription from Moab. It names Chemosh and several towns in this chapter, including Dibon, Nebo, Kiriathaim, Aroer, Jahaz and Kerioth. It shows Chemosh credited with Moab's victories over Israel.

insights.title: Borrowing from Isaiah and Numbers
insights.body: Much of this chapter echoes Isaiah's oracle on Moab, including the cries at Horonaim and the weeping for the vine of Sibmah (48:32). Verses 48:45-46 adapt an old song about Heshbon from Numbers. Jeremiah reworks earlier prophecy for his own day.

insights.title: Settled on his lees
insights.body: Moab has settled on his lees and not been poured from vessel to vessel (48:11). Winemakers poured wine off its sediment to keep it from spoiling. Moab, never exiled, has grown complacent, and God will send men to pour it out and smash its jars (48:12).

insights.title: Wordplay on place names
insights.body: Many lines play on Moabite town names in Hebrew. Madmen will be brought to silence, dimmah (48:2), and Moab is told to be like the juniper, aroer, a pun on the town Aroer (48:6). Such puns were a favorite prophetic device for oracles against towns.

insights.title: Ashamed like Bethel
insights.body: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was ashamed of Bethel (48:13). Bethel was the royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf. It failed to save Israel from Assyria.

insights.title: God weeps for Moab
insights.body: I will wail for Moab, and my heart sounds like pipes for Kir Heres (48:31, 48:36). God mourns even the enemy he judges, with flutes like those played at funerals. What does it say about God that he grieves for Israel's old foe?

insights.title: Moab restored
insights.body: Yet I will reverse the captivity of Moab in the latter days (48:47). The long oracle closes with hope. Ruth, the Moabite great-grandmother of David, already showed that Moab could be brought into God's people.

49.summary: Short oracles announce judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, the Arab tribes of Kedar and Hazor, and Elam, with promises of restoration for Ammon and Elam.
49.lookfor: Watch the different charge against each nation, the overlap with the book of Obadiah, and which nations receive a word of hope at the end.

names.name: Malcam
names.gloss: Milcom, the national god of Ammon; the name also sounds like their king.

names.name: Rabbah
names.gloss: The Ammonite capital, modern Amman in Jordan.

names.name: Teman
names.gloss: A region of Edom famous for its wise men.

names.name: Bozrah
names.gloss: A chief city of Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Arpad
names.gloss: A city-state in northern Syria.

names.name: Ben Hadad
names.gloss: A royal name used by several kings of Damascus.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: A powerful Arabian tribe of the Syrian desert.

names.name: Hazor
names.gloss: Here probably a name for the settlements of Arab tribes, not the city in Galilee.

insights.title: Ammon in Gad's land
insights.body: Has Israel no heir? Why does Malcam possess Gad? (49:1). After Assyria deported the tribes east of the Jordan in the 8th century BC, Ammon moved into Gad's territory. Malcam is Milcom, Ammon's god, though the Hebrew can also be read as their king.

insights.title: Edom and Obadiah
insights.body: Several verses on Edom, such as the grape gatherers and thieves (49:9) and the nest set high as an eagle's (49:16), closely match the opening of Obadiah. Scholars debate whether one prophet borrowed from the other or both used a common oracle. Both condemn Edom's pride.

insights.title: Wisdom in Teman
insights.body: Is wisdom no more in Teman? (49:7). Edom had a reputation for wisdom; Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite. Edom's rocky heights, where its people dwelled in the clefts of the rock (49:16), gave it a sense of security.

insights.title: Why Edom?
insights.body: The oracle gives pride as Edom's sin. Other biblical texts add that Edom rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall and took advantage of it. In the following centuries Edomites settled in southern Judah, the region later called Idumea.

insights.title: Mercy for orphans
insights.body: In the middle of the oracle against Edom comes an unexpected word: Leave your fatherless children. I will preserve them alive. Let your widows trust in me (49:11). Even in judgment, God claims to care for the most vulnerable of an enemy nation.

insights.title: Tents with no gates
insights.body: Kedar and Hazor are desert peoples who live in tents and have neither gates nor bars (49:29, 49:31). Hazor here probably means unwalled settlements of Arab tribes. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar raiding Arab tribes in the desert around 599 BC.

insights.title: The bow of Elam
insights.body: God will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might (49:35). Elam, east of Babylon, was famed for its archers. The oracle is dated to the start of Zedekiah's reign, 597 BC (49:34), when Elam may have been in conflict with Babylon.

insights.title: Restoration for some nations
insights.body: Ammon (49:6) and Elam (49:39) are both promised that God will reverse their captivity, as Moab and Egypt were. Edom, Damascus and Kedar are not. Luke lists Elamites among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost, which some readers see as an echo of this hope.

50.summary: Jeremiah announces that Babylon, the hammer of the whole earth, will fall to a nation from the north, its gods will be shamed, and the scattered people of Israel and Judah will return to Zion and be forgiven.
50.lookfor: Watch the role reversals (Babylon now facing a northern foe), the calls to flee, the promise of forgiveness, and the repeated sword in 50:35-38.

names.name: Bel
names.gloss: A title meaning lord, used for Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.

names.name: Merodach
names.gloss: Marduk, the patron god of the city of Babylon.

names.name: Merathaim
names.gloss: A region of southern Babylonia whose name is turned into a pun.

names.name: Pekod
names.gloss: An Aramean tribe in eastern Babylonia whose name is turned into a pun.

names.name: Carmel
names.gloss: The fertile mountain ridge on Israel's north coast.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: Rich pastureland east of the Sea of Galilee.

insights.title: The fall of Babylon
insights.body: Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC, less than fifty years after it destroyed Jerusalem. Babylonian and Persian records say the city was taken with little fighting, and Cyrus soon let exiles return home. The total desolation pictured here (50:13, 50:39) came gradually over the following centuries.

insights.title: Bel and Merodach shamed
insights.body: The oracle opens with Babylon's gods humiliated: Bel is disappointed, Merodach is dismayed (50:2). Marduk was the patron of Babylon, honored each year in the great New Year festival. When a city fell, its gods were thought to have failed or abandoned it.

insights.title: The north turns on Babylon
insights.body: For most of the book the foe from the north was Babylon. Now a nation from the north comes against Babylon (50:3, 50:9). Verses 50:41-43 repeat the description of the enemy in 6:22-24 almost exactly, now addressed to the daughter of Babylon, and 50:44-46 reuse lines first spoken against Edom.

insights.title: Lost sheep
insights.body: My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds led them astray (50:6). Their enemies excused themselves by saying Israel had sinned against Yahweh (50:7). Jesus spoke of being sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

insights.title: Flee from Babylon
insights.body: Flee out of the middle of Babylon! (50:8), like the male goats that lead the flock out of the fold. The call is repeated in chapter 51 and in Isaiah. Revelation applies it to God's people in the symbolic Babylon of its own day.

insights.title: Double rebellion and punishment
insights.body: Merathaim and Pekod (50:21) were real names in Babylonia, but in Hebrew merathaim sounds like double rebellion and peqod like punishment. The prophet names Babylon's regions for what they have earned.

insights.title: Sin sought and not found
insights.body: In those days Israel's iniquity will be sought for, and there will be none (50:20). The forgiveness is so complete that the record cannot be found. How does the promise to forgive sit alongside the call for vengeance on Babylon in the same chapter?

insights.title: A sword, and a drought
insights.body: A sword is on the Chaldeans, on her princes, her wise men, her mighty men, her horses and her treasures (50:35-37). Then a drought is on her waters (50:38). In Hebrew sword is herev and drought is horev, so the series ends with a pun. Babylon depended on irrigation from the Euphrates.

51.summary: The oracle against Babylon continues with the destroyer stirred up among the Medes, Babylon pictured as a golden cup and a broken hammer, and ends with Seraiah sinking a scroll of these words in the Euphrates.
51.lookfor: Watch the images of Babylon (cup, hammer, mountain, sea monster), the calls to God's people to leave, and the sign-act at the end.

names.name: Medes
names.gloss: A people of north-western Iran who joined with Persia to conquer Babylon.

names.name: Ararat
names.gloss: A kingdom in the mountains of eastern Turkey and Armenia, also called Urartu.

names.name: Minni
names.gloss: A kingdom near Lake Urmia in north-western Iran.

names.name: Ashkenaz
names.gloss: A people of the northern mountains, probably the Scythians.

names.name: Sheshach
names.gloss: A coded name for Babylon.

names.name: Lebkamai
names.gloss: A coded name for Chaldea, using the same letter-swap cipher as Sheshach.

names.name: Seraiah
names.gloss: Son of Neriah, Baruch's brother, a royal quartermaster.

names.name: Neriah
names.gloss: Father of Baruch and Seraiah.

insights.title: Kings of the Medes
insights.body: Yahweh has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes (51:11). The Medes destroyed Assyria together with Babylon, and later became part of Cyrus' Persian empire, which took Babylon in 539 BC. Isaiah too names the Medes as Babylon's destroyers.

insights.title: A golden cup
insights.body: Babylon has been a golden cup in Yahweh's hand, making all the earth drunk (51:7). Babylon was the instrument by which God gave the nations the cup of wrath. Revelation's Babylon holds a golden cup and makes the nations drink.

insights.title: The hammer of God
insights.body: You are my battle axe and weapons of war (51:20), and with you I shatter nations, horse and rider, shepherd and farmer, again and again in 51:20-23. Babylon was God's hammer. But the tool that broke others will itself be broken.

insights.title: Like the hymn of Jeremiah 10
insights.body: Verses 51:15-19 repeat the hymn of 10:12-16 about the God who made the earth by his power and is the portion of Jacob. Placed here, it reminds the reader why Babylon's idols cannot save it. Words from the book's middle are used again near its end.

insights.title: A sea monster swallows
insights.body: Nebuchadnezzar has swallowed me up like a monster and filled his belly (51:34). The Hebrew word can mean a sea serpent or dragon. Later God promises to make Bel, Babylon's god, give back what he has swallowed (51:44).

insights.title: Babylon's walls and river
insights.body: Babylon's broad walls will be utterly overthrown (51:58). Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon on a vast scale, with double walls, the Ishtar Gate, and the Euphrates flowing through the city. Ancient writers counted its walls among the wonders of the world. The prophet says it will all be for the fire.

insights.title: A scroll sunk in the Euphrates
insights.body: In Zedekiah's fourth year Jeremiah gives Seraiah a scroll of disasters against Babylon to read there and then tie to a stone and throw into the Euphrates (51:59-64). As the scroll sinks, so will Babylon. Revelation pictures an angel throwing a great millstone into the sea for Babylon's fall.

insights.title: Thus far the words
insights.body: The chapter ends: Thus far are the words of Jeremiah (51:64). The book's opening, the words of Jeremiah, finds its closing bracket here. Chapter 52 is an appendix, drawn mostly from 2 Kings, that records the fall of Jerusalem.

52.summary: An appendix retells the fall of Jerusalem: Zedekiah's rebellion and capture, the burning of the temple, the bronze furnishings carried off, the deportations, and Jehoiachin's release from prison in Babylon.
52.lookfor: Watch how closely this matches 2 Kings, the detailed list of temple objects, the numbers of exiles, and the last scene.

names.name: Riblah
names.gloss: Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters in Syria.

names.name: Nebuzaradan
names.gloss: Commander of Babylon's guard.

names.name: Seraiah
names.gloss: The chief priest, executed at Riblah; not the same Seraiah as in chapter 51.

names.name: Zephaniah
names.gloss: The second priest, also executed.

names.name: Jehoiachin
names.gloss: The king of Judah exiled to Babylon in 597 BC.

names.name: Evilmerodach
names.gloss: Amel-Marduk, Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, king 562–560 BC.

skim.advice: The inventory of bronze objects in 52:17-23 and the deportation figures in 52:28-30 can be read quickly; read closely the fall of the city and the closing release of Jehoiachin.

insights.title: Repeated from Kings
insights.body: Almost all of this chapter matches 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, apart from the deportation figures in 52:28-30. Editors placed it at the end of Jeremiah to show that his warnings came true. It also overlaps with Jeremiah 39.

insights.title: Burning the temple
insights.body: In the fifth month, Nebuzaradan burned Yahweh's house, the king's house and all the great houses (52:12-13). Jewish tradition remembers this on the ninth of Av, a fast day for the destruction of both the first and second temples. Kings dates the burning to the seventh day and Jeremiah to the tenth.

insights.title: The bronze treasures
insights.body: The two pillars, the bronze sea, the stands and many smaller vessels were broken up and carried off (52:17-23). Each pillar was eighteen cubits high, about eight metres, with capitals decorated with pomegranates. The bronze was so great it could not be weighed (52:20).

insights.title: Who was executed
insights.body: The chief priest Seraiah, the second priest Zephaniah, the three keepers of the threshold and other officials were executed at Riblah (52:24-27). Zephaniah had carried messages between Zedekiah and Jeremiah. Babylon removed the leadership that had backed the revolt.

insights.title: How many exiles?
insights.body: Jeremiah lists 3,023 deported in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 832 in his eighteenth and 745 in his twenty-third, 4,600 in all (52:28-30). Kings gives larger round figures for 597 BC, such as ten thousand. Jeremiah's numbers may count only adult men or a particular group; the exact basis is unknown.

insights.title: Jehoiachin's rations
insights.body: In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, about 561 BC, Evilmerodach released Jehoiachin from prison and gave him a regular allowance (52:31-34). Babylonian ration tablets from Nebuchadnezzar's palace list oil for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and his sons. The biblical detail of a royal allowance fits these records.

insights.title: An ending with a door ajar
insights.body: The book ends not with the burning but with David's heir eating at the king of Babylon's table (52:33). Nothing more is promised, but the line of David survives. Why might the editors have chosen this quiet note to close a book of judgment?

intro.who: Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, dictated many of his oracles to the scribe Baruch, and Jewish tradition in the Talmud credits him with the book. Most modern scholars see a book that grew over time from his poetic oracles, Baruch-style accounts of his life, and prose sermons shaped by later editors in the language of Deuteronomy.
intro.when: Jeremiah preached from about 627 BC, Josiah's thirteenth year, through Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC and on into exile in Egypt. The book's final shape dates from the exile or soon after; the Greek Septuagint preserves a shorter edition, about one-eighth shorter, with the oracles against the nations in a different place and order.
intro.why: It explains why Jerusalem fell, as the result of a covenant long broken, and records the costly life of the prophet who said so, while holding out God's promise to replant his people and make a new covenant written on the heart.
